text:
U.S. Rep. María Elvira Salazar is publicly challenging President Donald Trump over his administration's immigration enforcement policies in a new campaign advertisement released less than seven weeks before the midterm elections.

"Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," Salazar says at the beginning of the 30-second ad released Thursday.

The Republican congresswoman, who is seeking reelection in Florida's 27th Congressional District, is addressing an issue with particular significance in her Miami-area district, where nearly three-quarters of families are Hispanic, according to U.S. Census data.

The video is Salazar's first general-election advertisement of the 2026 campaign. She directly warns Trump about the impact his immigration policies could have on Hispanic voters.

"In July, 50% of the 50,000 people who were detained had no criminal record," Salazar says. "Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policies. The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."

Trump received approximately 57% of the 2024 presidential vote within the current boundaries of Florida's 27th Congressional District, compared with roughly 42% for Democrat Kamala Harris.

Barry University political science professor Sean Foreman called Salazar's decision to directly criticize a president from her own party notable.

"She seems to be confronting him on his immigration policies, and that is very rare for a sitting member of Congress to criticize their own president from their party," Foreman said.

Foreman said the message could be intended to reach independent and moderate voters who are dissatisfied with the administration's immigration policies.

"In order to win this race, she's trying to carve out some support from independents and moderates who might be very frustrated, even angry, by President Trump's immigration policy, which particularly is hitting very close to home here with the ending of TPS for Venezuelans and Haitians," Foreman said.

Salazar also uses the advertisement to appeal directly to Trump to take a different approach to immigration.

"You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery, and Reagan was for communism," Salazar says. "I'm not talking about giving them amnesty. I'm talking about giving them a dignified life in a promised land, and only you can do that."

Salazar has previously advocated for immigration legislation that would provide legal status to some undocumented immigrants who have lived in the United States for years, alongside border enforcement provisions.

Her Democratic opponent, former CBS News Miami anchor Eliott Rodriguez, criticized Salazar's message and her record on immigration.

"That video is mind-boggling," Rodriguez said. "Let's be clear: María Elvira Salazar is part of Donald Trump's immigration agenda. She tries to paint herself as an advocate and a champion of immigrants, but she votes contrary to that."

Rodriguez, who won the Democratic primary in August, said immigration and affordability drove him into the race.

Foreman said the move also carries political risks, particularly because Trump has endorsed her reelection campaign.

"We know how Donald Trump responds to criticism," Foreman said. "He doesn't like it, and he usually comes back even harder with criticism against the person and the thing they're criticizing about him."

As of Thursday, Trump had not publicly responded to Salazar's advertisement, according to multiple published reports.

CBS News Miami reached out to Salazar's campaign for comment about the advertisement but had not received a response.

text:
Grieving families are bringing their stories directly to Capitol Hill as the debate over sanctuary policies intensifies following another deadly case involving a person authorities say was in the country illegally.

Families who have lost loved ones described how immigration and sanctuary policies have affected their lives while urging Congress to change laws and policies that can restrict cooperation between local law enforcement agencies and federal immigration authorities.

One woman described losing her son and daughter-in-law just 16 days after the couple married.

"I thought I was taking my children to the safest place I could bring them," she said during testimony on Capitol Hill. "I did not realize that I was taking them to a state where sanctuary policies would then divide my life into before and after."

"Before, my son and daughter-in-law were married, and killed 16 days after they were married," she continued.

Their testimony comes as a separate tragedy in New Jersey puts renewed attention on the issue.

A 9-month-old boy was killed after authorities say a driver struck a mother and her two children in a grocery store parking lot. Officials have identified the driver as a person who was in the United States illegally.

The incident has prompted the mayor of Berkeley Township, Jennifer Bacchione, to call for changes to New Jersey's Immigrant Trust Directive, which limits the circumstances under which state and local law enforcement agencies can assist federal civil immigration enforcement.

Speaking with The National News Desk, Randy Sutton, a 33-year law enforcement veteran and founder and chairman of The Wounded Blue, argued sanctuary policies can create unnecessary public safety risks.

"It's shocking to see that we are looking at one more tragedy," Sutton said.

Sutton blamed the Biden administration's immigration policies and sanctuary jurisdictions for contributing to preventable crimes, describing the policies as a "continuing irresponsibility."

His comments represent his assessment of the connection between immigration policy and individual crimes. The immigration status of a suspect does not by itself establish that a particular government policy caused a crime, and research examining immigration and crime has produced a more complicated picture than individual high-profile cases may suggest.

For Sutton, one of the central issues is how local authorities respond when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement seeks custody of a person already being held in jail.

ICE detainers generally request that a law enforcement agency notify federal immigration officials before releasing certain noncitizens and, in some circumstances, maintain custody for a limited period to allow ICE to assume custody.

"The policies that have been working for years were detainers that ICE would put on people that were already in jail, who have already been arrested, so that they could safely take them and remove them from the country because they were illegal aliens," Sutton said.

Sanctuary policies vary considerably from one jurisdiction to another. Some restrict compliance with immigration detainers unless certain conditions are met, while others limit how local personnel or resources can be used for federal civil immigration enforcement.

Supporters of those policies argue that separating local policing from federal immigration enforcement can encourage undocumented residents to report crimes, cooperate with investigations and interact with police without fear of deportation.

Critics, including Sutton, argue those restrictions can result in removable noncitizens being released from local custody rather than transferred directly to ICE.

"What has happened is that these sanctuary cities, sanctuary states, have circumvented the ability for law enforcement to cooperate," Sutton said.

He argued the consequences extend beyond the potential release of individuals ICE wants to detain.

Sutton said requiring federal agents to locate and arrest someone after that person has returned to the community can create additional risks for both officers and the public.

"Law enforcement officers are placed in additional danger as well," Sutton said.

"They now have to go into the street in order to make arrests when they could have been done effectively and safely from the jails," he added.

Sutton said the issue should ultimately be viewed through the lens of public safety rather than partisan politics.

"This isn't about politics," he said. "This is about lifesaving."

His focus on dangers facing law enforcement officers is also central to his work with The Wounded Blue.

Sutton founded the national nonprofit to assist law enforcement officers who have suffered physical or psychological injuries in the line of duty, regardless of whether they work for federal, state or local agencies.

"The Wounded Blue is a nationwide charity that deals with injured and disabled officers no matter what their affiliation is — federal, state, local," Sutton said.

Sutton pointed to assaults and shootings involving police officers as evidence of the risks law enforcement personnel routinely encounter.

"You don't even see it on the news. You don't hear it anymore because it's become so commonplace," Sutton said.

The organization provides support to officers dealing with physical injuries as well as emotional and psychological trauma, he said.

Asked what specific policy change he would like to see, Sutton offered a straightforward answer.

"Simple cooperation," he said.

Sutton argued federal, state and local agencies need to be able to share information and coordinate when public safety is at stake.

"All law enforcement has to work together, whether it's federal task forces, whether it's local law enforcement working with state and local federal officers," he said.

"It has to be one synergistic type of environment where everybody works together for the common good, and that is the public safety."

The debate over sanctuary policies has persisted for years because it involves competing questions about federal immigration authority, state and local control, constitutional limits, community trust and public safety.

Federal courts have also placed legal limits on how immigration detainers can be implemented, meaning the dispute is not simply a question of whether local governments want to cooperate with ICE. The details of individual state laws, detention requests and court rulings can determine what local agencies are legally permitted or required to do.

But for families who have lost loved ones, the debate is far less abstract.

Their testimony on Capitol Hill is intended to put individual names and stories behind a policy fight often discussed through statistics and political arguments.

And for Sutton, the central question is whether different levels of law enforcement have the ability to work together before another tragedy occurs.

"Everybody works together for the common good," Sutton said. "And that is the public safety."

text:
This year, on his way to the library or the gym, Varina resident Paul Fleisher witnessed unmarked airplanes as well as planes with company logos that aren’t featured as commercial carriers at Richmond International Airport, parked on the quiet, far eastern end of the facility behind a chain-linked fence.

White school buses were there to meet the ABX Air, Global X and Eastern Air Express flights where shackled people ascended a movable walkway onto the planes.

The remote activity became clear.

These operations were ICE detainee-transfer flights carrying people out of state, far from family and legal representation, to detention hubs in Louisiana, Texas or California, where some ultimately may be placed aboard removal flights to other countries.

In some cases, deportees from airports throughout the United States are being jailed indefinitely in prisons in their countries of origin or flown to other countries where they are not citizens, according to cases documented by Human Rights First.

“It reminded me of internment of Japanese Americans during World War Two. I compare it to the Holocaust and the entire slave trade. These people could be considered to be kidnapping victims,” Fleisher said.

Much of the detainee movement occurs outside ordinary public view.

“The entire business of how they are treating our immigrant neighbors is horrific. Families are being separated. People are being shuffled so they can’t get legal representation. I’m disgusted by the way my own country is treating our immigrant folks.”

Fleisher is not alone in his concerns.

On Saturday, Fleisher and other activists who are a part of RVA Indivisible (RVA ICE-Scream, the First Unitarian Universalist Church and other groups) are gathering at a busy intersection by RIC to act as a witness to the deportation flights and to “demand an end to these cruel and unlawful deportations.”

The protest will take place at the corner of Williamsburg Road and Airport Drive in Sandston.

One person who plans to attend commented they see RIC as complicit in the growing number of flights.

“DHS is disappearing our neighbors. Don’t let them use our airport to do it,” the commenter wrote online.

Grave human rights abuses

While detentions and deportations in the Richmond area and throughout Virginia have not been marked by the widely viewed violence and resistance as in Chicago’s Operation Midway Blitz and Minneapolis’ Metro Surge, they have been significant.

The Deportation Data Project counted 20,240 people arrested by ICE in Virginia since January 2023, whether or not the arrest resulted in a decision to detain that person. Nationwide, DDP has counted 896,393 ICE arrests between October 2022 and August 2026.

Dataset graphs show a significant spike in ICE action in Virginia, as in the rest of the country.

From October 2022 through December 2024, ICE averaged about 150 arrests per month in Virginia, according to Deportation Data Project. Since January 2025, the monthly average has risen to roughly five times that level.

In July alone, there were 49,571 ICE arrests nationwide, which exceeds the December 2025 number of 40,177. In Virginia that number was 805, which was 200 fewer people apprehended than the previous month.

According to the Human Rights First nonprofit ICE deportation tracker’s latest report, Richmond International Airport has played a key role in deportation shuffle flights to deportation hubs in Louisiana.

The flights Fleisher sees come and go with regularity.

This year, RIC has received 132 domestic shuffle flights transporting shackled detainees out of Virginia. HRF’s new ICE Flight Monitor interactive dashboard shows how regularly the domestic transfer flights arrive and depart from RIC thrice weekly, often with detainees from preceding segments held in shackles for extended hours.

HRF counts Richmond as one of the five U.S. cities seeing more than 50% more shuffle flights than the previous month, with 27 in August, 25 flights in July and 16 flights in June. From January to May 2026, there were either 12 or 13 ICE deportation flights at the airport.

These flights previously were met right in front of the Fixed Base Operator terminal of Richmond Jet Center, but an employee of the business said the flights were moved away from the terminal because of what the employee described as the “sensitive” nature of the operation.

HRF counted a total of 128 deportation flights out of Richmond airport in 2025, more than two-and-a-half times the number of flights in 2024 (50).

The local deportation shuffle flight operation, while considered “sparse” in the scheme of flights at RIC, is a part of federal priorities to “pursue an unprecedented mass deportation agenda” as described extensively in HRF. To date, HRF has tracked nearly 64,000 flights since 2020.

This August, HRF calculated a total of 1,267 domestic shuffle flights nationwide – a 58% increase from the same month last year.

Federal funding for immigration enforcement has increased substantially under the Trump administration. The 2025 reconciliation law provided nearly $75 billion in additional funding to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, including $45 billion to expand immigration detention capacity.

In 2026, Congress approved another roughly $70 billion through the Secure America Act for immigration and border enforcement across ICE, U.S. Customs and Border Protection and the Department of Homeland Security. That measure included approximately $38 billion for ICE and $26 billion for CBP, with additional funding provided to DHS for related enforcement activities.

ICE reported 442,637 removals and returns during fiscal year 2025, substantially exceeding the 175,000 target identified in its congressional budget documents. Because the federal fiscal year ran from Oct. 1, 2024 through Sept. 30, 2025, however, that total spans two presidential administrations, including the final months of the Biden administration and more than eight months of the Trump administration.

For fiscal years 2026 and 2027, ICE has established a much higher target of 1 million returns and removals annually. The agency defines its removal statistics to include formal removals as well as certain returns, including voluntary returns and voluntary departures, while its detention figures measure initial bookings into ICE facilities. The increased removal target is part of the Trump administration's broader expansion of immigration enforcement.

In its report, Human Rights First characterizes a number of ICE tactics as unlawful and cruel.

Human Rights First has raised concerns that ICE’s rapidly expanding detention and transfer system can make it more difficult for detainees to remain in contact with family members and attorneys and to pursue their immigration cases.

The organization also has documented cases in which the federal government has sought to deport people to third countries where they are not citizens, sometimes despite claims that they could face persecution, torture or other serious harm. Advocates have argued that rapid transfers between detention facilities and removals with limited notice can interfere with detainees’ ability to obtain legal assistance or seek habeas corpus relief – the legal process through which a person can challenge the lawfulness of detention.

'Silence equals consent'

Many, like Fleisher do not see the point of targeting immigrants they describe as law-abiding, who they say have come here to work – some of whom already had cases in the immigration system.

“Our country’s economy relies on what these people do. Our economy relies on the taxes they generate. They get no benefit,” Fleisher opined. “I’m disgusted by the way my own country is treating our immigrant folks.”

Fleisher said he contacted the 14-member Capital Region Airport Commission and was told that because RIC accepts federal grants and operates as a commercial airport, it is obligated to accept legal flights.

“They can’t just deny landing rights just because they don’t like what they are doing,” Fleisher said.

Fleisher wants to address the Capital Region Airport Commission at one of its monthly meetings, but though those meetings are open to the public, Fleisher said he was told that CRAC's regular meetings do not include a general public-comment period.

“As a public body using our public funds, it ought to have a time for public comment,” Fleisher said.

A year ago, when the deportation flights came to light through reporting in the Citizen, their presence was news to CRAC members. The commission is composed of representatives appointed by Henrico, Chesterfield and Hanover counties and the City of Richmond.

“Silence equals consent,” Fleisher said. “I don’t consent, and I have been pretty vocal about that and condemning the Trump administration. I have no intention to be quiet.”

Requests to ICE for information about the organization behind the Richmond International Airport deportation flights, as well as the backgrounds of the people being transported on them, their charges and their ultimate destinations, went unanswered.

But officials from ICE and the Department of Homeland Security have publicly defended the administration’s increased immigration enforcement as an effort to enforce federal immigration laws, remove people who are subject to removal and protect public safety.

ICE officials have said that detention is used to ensure some people appear for immigration proceedings, facilitate removals and address cases in which criminal histories may present public-safety risks. The agency also uses alternatives to detention for some people who remain in their communities while their cases proceed.

Administration officials have frequently emphasized arrests of immigrants with criminal records, but ICE enforcement is not limited to people convicted of crimes: people may be placed in removal proceedings based on alleged violations of immigration law, such as entering the country without authorization or overstaying a visa.

For daughter trying to locate father, 'I feel like there's nothing in my control'

Last fall when Henrico resident Rosa Lobo received a call from her father, she didn’t initially answer because she had started her workday. But the call proved urgent.

He, along with his whole work crew, had been picked up by ICE around Washington, D.C. Born in El Salvador, Rosa’s father did not have a permit to work and live here. He was brought here as a child and has lived here since.

She described her father as someone who felt American.

“He has an accent, but he speaks English pretty well,” said Lobo, who was born in Southwest Virginia. “He speaks Spanish, which is his first language. He's a very silly, goofy guy when you meet him, but he's not stupid. He knows what's going on. He knows what people think about him. He watches the news, he's very studious. He's very religious. He'll read his Bible every night before he goes to bed. He is good at defusing situations.”

Then Gabriel Lobo was in detention at an ICE center in Chantilly, Virginia.

After that, he was transferred to the Farmville ICE Detention Center, where Rosa went to visit him.

She set up a GoFundMe to raise funds for legal support which grew donations due to her connections in the Richmond area as a graduate of a local prestigious university and an impactful nonprofit. She credits the Richmond Legal Aid Justice Center, Richmond Legal Fund and the Amica Center with supporting her and her father as much as they could.

She is just one of dozens of other area residents who have created GoFundMe fundraising campaigns to pay for legal support in a federal immigration system in which people generally do not have a right to government-appointed counsel. Thousands across the country have used the platform to garner help for their family members.

Seeing her normally tidy father shackled and disheveled shook Rosa to her core.

Soon, her father was gone, flown out in the middle of the night to a Louisiana detention center.

In Louisiana, he was again in the middle of the night loaded onto a plane – this time flown to El Salvador, where she said he ended up in CECOT (Centro de Confinamiento del Terrorismo), a maximum-security prison built by the Salvadoran government as part of its campaign against gangs.

Rosa worried as communication stopped.

The experience has taken a toll on Rosa's mental health. The tense situation and fear during this administration remind her of her mother's experiences growing up in Southwest Virginia watching the Klan march in her town.

"We think about these things as being so far away and so out of reach. But, it's recent history. It's things that my parents remember and things that are happening actively to me, to people younger than me," Rosa said.

“I'm so tired, and I feel like there's nothing in my control.”

Her family hired lawyers in El Salvador to free her father, but he was caught in a prison system from which he could not secure his release (though she said he had committed no crime there), due to that country’s “state of exception.”

That, according to human-rights organizations, has permitted authorities in the nation to detain people for extended periods based on suspected gang affiliation with severely limited due-process protections.

“I've had to swallow the fact that there's a high possibility I'm never going to see my dad again,” Rosa said. “Even if he lives. There's a 0% chance that he's going to be able to come back to the United States. Whether or not I would be able to travel to El Salvador is up in the air as well.

“It's a good chance that I'm not going to see him again, be it because he's detained indefinitely because he needs to keep a low profile and stay in El Salvador, or be it because he is fully disappeared and possibly killed. I don't know. It's truly a hopeless situation at this point.”

The mental toll on Rosa has been significant. While worrying if her father is being treated inhumanely, she forces herself to eat, sleep and work, finding solace with activism with the Democratic Socialists.

“I've tried reaching out to my elected officials, not about my case in particular, but about the subject as a whole, signing petitions, sending letters, about something has to be done about ICE. Something has to be done about this mass disappearing of people in the United States. But every response, it's always, like the automatic ones you get from their desk, ‘Thank you for reaching out to your representative. So-and-so in the office saw your letter and this is what they had to say.’ And it's always ‘We'll get around to it.’”

In the spring, Rosa’s GoFundMe update showed her father’s status as still jailed in El Salvador without charges being pressed.

“These days, the only evidence I have that my father is even alive is that someone spends the money my uncle sends in for his food,” wrote Rosa, noting that any legal process there could take years.

She still does not know what he was charged with in the U.S.

Mugshots bear witness

Radio Poder Spanish-language morning-show radio host Oscar Contreras prays for and with his listeners daily from a quiet radio station office in a nondescript Henrico office park building.

But during the past two years, the station’s social media page took a diversion from uplifting community events and educational opportunities with inspiring Biblical verses.

As ICE apprehensions began to increase, his listeners started calling him for help.

“People were calling me saying 'My family member was taken. I don't know where he is,'” Contreras said. “It was kind of like kidnapping.”

So, Contreras, who was born in Guatemala and is a U.S. citizen, began searching.

Mugshot websites helped him find people who had been detained – photos of Latinos and Latinas in workwear of those who toil outside in landscaping, house painting, roofing and in kitchens photographed at their worst moment.

“When I find out that this page, you could find the people and let the family members know, I was able to help the families find the people because I have their birthdays,” Contreras said.

“I said, ‘I don't think people know this. I didn't know this.’ I didn’t know there were so many detentions. I thought like one here, one there, because you would expect things to be on video, but it was happening. I thought, ‘What do I do with this information?’”

A short hesitation of posting photos meant to embarrass the person who allegedly committed a violation is now a visual witness to Virginia’s role in a nationwide mass deportation effort.

Contreras offers to remove photos if the people or families contact him. He also posts from the bustednewspapers.com website: "The people registered are representative of that entry, not of their guilt or innocence. Every person arrested is presumed innocent until proven guilty."

He has sifted through the mugshots of those detained at Riverside Regional Jail and now Chesapeake City Jail stating: “Several people detained by ICE are registered in prisons before being taken to Detention Centers. Usually the information says: Arrested by ICE but we are publishing the people with Latin American names because this prison is used by ICE. (NOT ALL WERE REGISTERED BY ICE, BUT IT IS DIFFICULT TO SAY AT LEAST THAT THEY SPECIFY)”

He saw sadness, confusion and uncertainty in their faces.

Stories Contreras hears are heartbreaking:

• a family member searching for four members of her family who were apprehended as they were out fishing.

• a pregnant mother who was left with four other children, asking for assistance.

• a woman whose husband was caught by ICE who had to abandon his work truck in a random neighborhood asked for help searching for their property.

• a child of a deported parent who refused to go to school after being bullied. Contreras set up a meeting with the school to get home instruction for the student.

“Children have to go to school after their parents were taken. It's a lot to carry. People may say, ‘They're criminal.’ Okay, fine. But it doesn't diminish the suffering of the people,” Contreras said. (A Brookings Institution analysis estimated that about 145,000 U.S. citizen children had experienced the detention of a parent between January 2025 and April 2026.)

• a woman whose mugshot Contreras posted later called asking him to take it down after she was released from detention telling of torturous conditions.

“I asked, can you share your story?” Contreras said. “She was telling me, 'I'm traumatized by it.' It was extremely cold and one of the detentions that she was in, the bathrooms had plugged up, and because of it, the women were doing their business on the floor because there were no restrooms. They were moved four or five times, not just plane flights. She said there was a group of women where they would come to them and say, ‘Okay, you're gonna be transported,’ and then we just put them in the van, take them, and at the end of the day, they were being brought back.”

The woman told Contreras that the experience continues to disrupt her sleep and makes it difficult for her to leave her home.

Reactions to the mugshots on Radio Poder’s social media have varied. Some people have said “Great this is what I wanted.”

One commenter lamented: “How sad because most are not doing anything wrong, just looking for a living for their families.”

Contreras’ connection to churches resulted in meetings of congregations that wanted to become more informed about the impact of deportations on immigrant communities and to help those who are detained and those left behind.

“The result has been in large and small ways,” Contreras said. “In small ways, I can tell people that I'm praying for them, and listen to them. And the big way, there are churches and organizations that are working together and connecting to see how they can help the immigrant community. I think that's a good thing that came from this initiative of like, ‘Hey, something's happening, and people have to come together.’”

With the awareness of the ICE activity, lawyers on Radio Poder have encouraged adults to get their power of attorney documents in order to protect their children.

Contreras thinks Virginia’s elected leaders need to publicly acknowledge the high numbers of detainments and deportations and the impact on the community.

“I think that would be a huge start,” Contreras said. “If someone like our governor or our federal officials would say, ‘Yes, this is happening,’ then at least you know that they know, and then, hopefully, they'll do something about it. And you can be like, ‘Well, you know all the details, you know, so stop it.’”

text:
WASHINGTON — The White House said Thursday that it was withdrawing its nomination of Lance Schroyer, a former Oklahoma state trooper, to lead U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, ensuring that an agency at the forefront of President Donald Trump’s domestic agenda will remain without a Senate-confirmed leader for at least a while longer.

Schroyer is close to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, a former U.S. senator from Oklahoma. He has little experience with immigration.

The White House offered no comment in a brief statement. When he nominated Schroyer in June, Trump said on his Truth Social platform that his pick was “a PATRIOT with real operational experience” and a “proven leader with DECADES of experience locking up the worst of the worst.”

ICE has not had a Senate-confirmed leader since the Obama administration. David Venturella returned to the agency as acting director earlier this year after Todd Lyons resigned.

United States Institute of Peace files emergency motion to block carving of Trump's name on its facade

While Donald Trump ponders demolishing the Kennedy Center unless his name is added to the memorial for the slain president, the United States Institute of Peace filed an emergency motion in federal court on Thursday asking a judge to block his administration “from carrying out plans to carve President Trump’s name into the façade of the iconic USIP headquarters building.”

The filing was made in a court battle that began in May 2025, when a federal judge ruled that Elon Musk’s so-called “department of government efficiency”, or US Doge service, illegally took over the the non-profit thinktank created and funded by the US Congress through “blunt force, backed up by law enforcement officers from three separate local and federal agencies”.

Musk’s Doge staff fired most USIP employees in a late-night email in March 2025, and then forcefully entered the thinktank’s building after cancelling its contract for private security.

In court, the USIP has maintained the organization is an independent creation of Congress and outside the president’s executive authority. The administration argues it is an executive branch organization, and pushed ahead, last December, with affixing Trump’s name to the exterior of the building, using bolted-on lettering. That change already offended the USIP board members who filed the suit, but carving Trump’s name into the stone, they argued on Thursday, “would cause irreparable harm”.

In the new filing, lawyers for the USIP argue that the administration, including Trump and his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, have not followed the court’s order to maintain the status quo at the institute:

double quotation markRather, they continued to dismantle USIP and to actively undermine the organizational independence enshrined in USIP’s organic statute— including by affixing the President’s name to the building. Unsatisfied with the relative impermanence of external lettering, Appellants apparently now intend to carve President Trump’s name into the façade of USIP’s privately owned headquarters building while this litigation is pending. The building—which was largely funded by private donations to USIP as a tax exempt nonprofit corporation— is a work of expressive architecture designed to be “symbolic of USIP’s “independent “mission.”

Canvasser knocking on doors to support Susan Collins caught on camera stealing package from outside home

A canvasser for a Maine political action committee who was paid to knock on doors in support of Republican senator Susan Collins faces criminal charges after being caught on a doorbell camera stealing a package from an absent homeowner’s porch in Woolwich, Maine on Wednesday afternoon.

Video of the man, dressed in a red T-shirt with the name of the PAC, Stronger Maine, on the front and the name of the candidate, Susan Collins, on the back went viral after it was posted on Facebook by the homeowner.

Stronger Maine called the police and fired the canvasser immediately, a source who has worked with the group told the Bangor Daily News.

The Collins campaign said that the man was not employed by them.

According to Federal Election Commission records, more than half of Stronger Maine’s $2.6m in fundraising this year has come from from the Virginia-based conservative dark-money group Stronger America, which donated $1.4m.

Andy O’Brien, the former managing editor of a Rockland, Maine newspaper, pointed out on social media that the canvasser did a poor job of covering his tracks, because, before he grabbed the package and ran to his car, he left a flyer for Collins hanging on the homeowner’s front door.

The canvasser, who appeared to have the Latin phrase “Si vis pacem, para bellum” (“If you want peace, prepare for war”) tattooed on his right arm, was later identified by the police and faces charges.

“Thank you Woolwich residents and Facebook detectives,” the local shariff’s office said in a statement on Thursday. “The package thief/political campaigner has been identified and charges will be forthcoming.”

The US Postal Service has stopped work on developing a computer system that was central to Donald Trump’s effort to limit mail voting after the supreme court rejected the planned to change to how mail ballots are delivered this week, postmaster general David Steiner told the Associated Press.

“There’s an injunction so we’re not doing anything,” postmaster general David Steiner said in an interview.

Steiner, a former chief executive of Waste Management, Inc, said he is pressing Congress for changes that would help him resolve what he has called a “liquidity crisis.”

Trump’s efforts to largely eradicate mail voting would have turned the postal service into an arbiter of who is eligible to vote just months before this year’s midterm elections.

Steiner declined to take a position on Trump’s policy, presenting himself as the leader of an “independent agency of the executive branch” whose influence over the president’s order was limited to operational concerns.

“I don’t get to decide what rules that are put on us that I decide to accept or not accept,” he said.

'I don’t know what the hell that means', Trump says of executive order he signed to let hunters use lead ammunition

Donald Trump signed a pair of executive orders to expand hunting and fishing on Thursday which, he told a gathering of outdoor industry leaders in the White House Rose Garden, mean “opening up millions of acres of federal land for our hunters and fishers.”

The orders seek to expand fresh and saltwater fishing and direct the secretary of the interior and other federal agencies to find ways to expand hunting, including of species not subject to certain endangered protection laws, within 90 days.

Those agencies will then have 180 days to propose rollbacks to federal restrictions against hunting and fishing on federal land and to find ways to expand using that land for recreation.

“This builds on our actions in August that opened up another 92 million acres of federal land across 32 states,” Trump said in remarks he largely read, and even hinted he did not entirely understand.

“We believe that public lands belong to the American people and to the public and hunters, fishers, and outdoorsmen should be able to access them and they weren’t able to,” Trump read aloud from a text he suggested his interior secretary, Doug Burgum, had prepared for him. “And this order also protects the use of affordable, traditional le-” Trump read, and then stopped to comment on what were supposed to be his own remarks.

“Well, this is pretty good. Is that- I never knew this was a problem, Doug. You’re going to have to educate me, but you put it in,” he said to Burgum, before continuing to read the text: “lead ammunition.”

The president then paused and looked up again to comment: “Is ammunition, lead ammunition was a problem, huh? Is it better than other ammunition? I assume, huh? That’s uh pretty good. I don’t know what the hell that means, but I know one thing: you wanted it, you wanted it, and I’m here for you,” he told the industry leaders assembled before him, who burst into applause.

“So, the order protects the use of affordable traditional lead ammunition,” Trump continued reading.

“That sounds good to me,” he said.

As Trump spoke, the website of the US Fish and Wildlife Service, an agency within the Department of the Interior, still officially encouraged hunters to go “lead-free”, urging hunters to take advantage of “Lead-free ammunition incentives available at 26 refuges across 19 states” for the 2026–2027 hunting season.

“Protect wildlife by choosing lead-free ammunition this hunting season. Encourage other hunters to choose lead-free ammunition for all hunting, including big game,” the agency urged hunters, as of Thursday night.

The agency’s website even answers the question Trump apparently failed to ask: “Why choose lead-free hunting ammunition?” with the following information – now apparently to be discarded at his order:

double quotation markLead fragments on impact. Lead ammunition loses weight as small pieces strip from the front of the bullet or shot as it passes through an animal. These fragments are found farther from the wound channel than you may expect, and many are too small to see with the naked eye, making them difficult to remove.

Fragments reach scavengers. Lead fragments may be left in the remains after harvesting an animal, even after field dressing. Remains from field-dressed animals provide a food source for scavenging wildlife, including bald and golden eagles.

Lead-free ammunition leaves less behind. When ingested, a lead fragment no bigger than a grain of rice can sicken and even kill an animal the size of a bald eagle. Lead-free ammunition leaves little or no fragments behind that could be consumed by scavenging wildlife.

Latvia bans Russian oligarch who paid for Donald Trump Jr's wedding party, Umar Kremlev, and hockey star Alex Ovechkin

Latvia’s foreign minister, Baiba Braže, has declared two Russian nationals, Alexander Ovechkin and Umar Kremlev, personae non gratae, meaning that they are banned from entering the country.

As the Guardian reported, Ovechkin, the NHL’s all-time leading goalscorer, appeared last week in a campaign ad for United Russia, Vladimir Putin’s parliamentary party, before returning to the US for another season as captain on the Washington Capitals.

ProPublica revealed this week that Kremlev, a Putin-connected boxing official, paid for, and attended, Donald Trump Jr’s wedding celebration on a private island in the Bahamas in May.

In a letter to the NHL’s commissioner made public on Wednesday, a Republican congressman from South Carolina, Joe Wilson, expressed “serious concern” over Ovechkin lending his celebrity to support “the dictatorial political party of Russian war criminal Vladimir Putin, who actively works to oppress the people of Russia by outlawing freedom of speech and fair elections.”

Ovechkin, a longtime supporter of Putin, whose Instagram profile picture shows him with the Russian president, has attempted to cast his appearance in the party’s video as a patriotic act. In a statement to the media, the Capitals said that Ovechkin, while in Russia, “was asked by his country to participate in a video campaign”, without acknowledging that it was a partisan political ad not for the nation of Russia, but for the party supporting its dictatorial president who has waged a brutal war of aggression against Ukraine.

On Thursday, Ovechkin responded to questions about his appearance in the campaign video with Russia’s foreign minister, Sergey Lavrov, the leading parliamentary candidate on the party’s list for upcoming elections, by saying, “I’m Russian and I support my country.”

“I’m for peace and love,” he added. “They asked me to do that, and I said yes.”

According to Meduza, an independent Russian news outlet based in Latvia, Putin’s political team first considered making Ovechkin a candidate for United Russia in the 2026 elections.

The Russian business news outlet RBC reported that when Russia’s state-owned polling firm tested the hockey star’s potential candidacy, they found that he would have been more popular than three of the top five candidates who were eventually selected.

“His results were decent,” a source close to Putin’s administration working on United Russia’s campaign told Meduza. “But not good enough for anyone to ask him specifically or force him to do it. And he didn’t want to do it. He understood it would take a lot of time… appearing in a video is easy”.

Democrats point out Florida Republican was actually for Trump's immigration enforcement drive before she was against it

As our colleague Chris Stein reports, congresswoman María Elvira Salazar, a Florida Republican, released a campaign ad recorded outside the White House in which she told Donald Trump that some of his “immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” and warned him that he is alienating Hispanics who supported him in 2024.

Salazar is facing a tough re-election fight in a Miami-area district that is nearly three-quarters Hispanic, where recent polling shows her tied with her Democratic challenger Eliott Rodriguez, a former television news anchor.

Democrats responded to the ad by casting doubt on Salazar’s apparent break with Trump over immigration enforcement.

On social media, the Democratic party’s main account shared video of the congresswoman telling NBC News in April: “we have to fund ICE and DHS – ICE and Border Patrol.”

“Don’t fall for her lies. María Elvira Salazar has stood with ICE every step of the way,” the Democrats said in a caption to the clip of her April remarks supporting ICE funding.

Salazar was speaking at the time about the ultimately successful Republican effort to pass a $70bn bill to fund Trump’s crackdown on undocumented immigrants through the end of his term.

When that funding bill narrowly passed the House in June, in a 214-212 vote, Salazar cast a crucial vote in favor of the measure to allocate $38bn to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), $26bn to Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and $5bn more to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) through September 2029.

Aaron Fritschner, an aide to Democratic congressman Don Beyer, commented on Salazar’s criticism of Trump’s immigration crackdown: “Salazar is correct about this but she is saying it to Trump in a campaign ad for her reelection after silently empowering harm and suffering for two years and voters aren’t going to be fooled about what she is doing or why she’s doing it”.

Judge orders Kennedy Center to give 30-day notice before any major renovations... or demolition

Not long after President Trump threatened to tear down the Kennedy Center unless his administration is allowed to slap his name on it, a federal judge on Thursday ordered him to hit the brakes.

The order from U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper mandated that the Kennedy Center tip off the public at least 30 days before making any significant changes to the structure – such as demolishing it.

The center is currently closed due to what its Trump-backed leadership calls safety issues caused by age and structural deficiencies.

But opponents fear that closing the center is a pretext for its demolition, or retaliation for Trump not being allowed to follow through on a plan for renovations that would see his name added to former President John F. Kennedy’s on the building’s facade.

Trump has done a lot to stoke those anxieties recently. In addition to his recent remarks, the president was photographed on Air Force One reviewing what appeared to be plans for the center’s demolition.

The White House on Thursday announced that it had withdrawn its nomination for Lance Schroyer, who President Trump had picked months earlier to serve as the new head of Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

A former Oklahoma state trooper, Schroyer faced criticism for his apparent lack of formal experience working in ICE. His greatest connection to the agency appeared to be his previous stint on the security detail of Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary Trump chose to replace the ousted Kristi Noem.

A White House statement announcing the withdrawal of Schroyer’s nomination gave no reason for the move.

Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Trump’s Health and Human Services Secretary and a longtime champion of the anti-vaccine movement, on Thursday addressed Children’s Health Defense, the anti-vaccine advocacy organization he ran for years.

On stage at the organization’s event in Washington D.C., Kennedy touted his efforts to bring his agency’s force to bear on vaccines and processed food.

“For many years, you’ve asked questions from outside the government, as I did,” Kennedy said in a meandering hour-and-a-half-long speech. “And now I have the privilege and the responsibility of leading the department that can put the full weight of the federal government behind answering those questions.”

He continued: “That’s what this department has done for the past 19 months, under my leadership, and under the leadership of President Trump.”

Kennedy reassured the audience that he would continue to represent their interests, and that they “have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House.” He touched only once on the measles outbreak that recently killed four people in Pennsylvania, arguing that Americans should care about children “who are dying or suffering or being injured by vaccine injuries” as much as those who die of infectious diseases.

Jon Kyl, a longtime Republican congressman from Arizona, died on Thursday, his family said in a statement.

Over three decades in Congress – first as a member of the House of Representatives, and later of the Senate – Kyl established himself as a quiet titan of Arizona politics. His family attributed his cause of death to complications from a neurological disease.

Kyl announced in a statement late last year that he would be withdrawing from public life after being “diagnosed with a neurological disease manifesting as dementia.”

“We know that Jon belonged to all of Arizona, a state he loved and explored with vigor, curiosity, and wonder,” Kyl’s family said in the statement. “Serving his state and nation in Congress was a privilege and responsibility he honored and respected. We are grateful for his full and meaningful public life.”

Kyl first joined the House of Representatives in 1987, an office he held before winning election to the Senate in 1995. He held his Senate seat until his retirement 2013, briefly returning by appointment in 2018 after the death of fellow Arizona senator John McCain.

House Republican releases campaign ad critical of Trump’s immigration policies

Chris Stein

A Republican congresswoman has released a campaign ad criticizing Donald Trump’s approach to immigration enforcement, in the latest sign that a key plank of the president’s 2024 re-election campaign has become a liability for his congressional allies ahead of November’s midterm elections.

“Mr President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” Florida’s María Elvira Salazar says in a 30-second ad. “In July, 50% of the 50,000 people that were detained had no criminal record. Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy.”

Salazar represents a competitive Miami-area district that is nearly three-quarters Hispanic, and where Trump won by a 15-point margin two years ago after a campaign in which he promised to carry out “mass deportations”. While his administration has implied that those targeted would be undocumented immigrants who committed crimes in the United States, in reality, a substantial portion of the people arrested since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 have no criminal record.

Salazar won re-election by a 20-point margin in 2024, but this year is facing a significant challenge from Eliott Rodriguez, the Democratic nominee and a former television news anchor. A poll conducted for his campaign late last month found him tied with Salazar.

“The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” Salazar said in the ad. “You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism. I’m not talking about giving them amnesty. I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land.”

Salazar’s ad is the latest instance of Republican lawmakers seeking to put distance between themselves and Trump before the 3 November elections, in which Democrats are vying to take back both the House and Senate. With gas prices high due to the war with Iran and Trump’s public approval low – including on key issues like handling of immigration – Democrats increasingly believe their candidates are competitive even in heavily Republican seats.

Kennedy Center says building closed temporarily due to 'acute risks to public safety'

A top official at the Kennedy Center said that he closed the institution temporarily due to “acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration” of the aging building.

Matt Floca, the Kennedy Center’s executive director and chief operating officer, said in a federal court filing seen by the Associated Press that the building will be closed for at least seven days to “assess existing safety risks in those portions of the main building exhibiting severe structural deterioration”.

The temporary closure, which occurred without notice yesterday, is separate from a vote on Tuesday by the Kennedy Center’s Trump-picked board to close the performing arts center indefinitely for repairs.

It was based on an inspection of the roof terrace canopy and a partial ceiling collapse earlier this month, Floca said. The closure may be extended after evaluation next week, he said.

The announcement of the closure came in response to a court case filed by Democratic congresswoman, Joyce Beatty, who is a trustee and sought an emergency court hearing to prevent what she called the building’s “unlawful closing’.

Beatty, an Ohio Democrat and an ex-officio member of the Kennedy Center board, has led efforts to block Donald Trump’s name from being added to the facade of the building. Beatty told MSNOW she had a verbal confrontation with the president on Tuesday during a virtual board meeting.

The Trump-aligned board, chaired by the president, voted to close the center after a federal judge blocked the institution from returning Trump’s name to the building.

Trump, who was named the Kennedy Center’s chairman last year by loyalists on the board, said yesterday that his efforts to restore the aging building deserve recognition, “because frankly, if we don’t do that, it’s going to close. It’ll end up being ripped down. It’s in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape.”

Congress has allocated $257m to cover the repairs, but Trump said they only would happen if the board was permitted to move forward with plans to add his name to the building.

Anti-vaccine advocates take victory lap ahead of address from RFK Jr. in D.C.

Melody Schreiber

As the death toll from the worst measles outbreak in decades mounts, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is headlining the Washington, D.C., conference of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense, which he led for nearly two decades.

Longtime anti-vaccine activists celebrated their unprecedented role in the national conversation, at times expressing astonishment over the ways anti-vaccine sentiment has been elevated to the highest levels of the US government.

Kennedy, now serving as secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), brings unusual attention to the conference, said Mary Holland, current CEO of Children’s Health Defense (CHD). “We have an opportunity today to speak to our colleagues and our friends in mainstream media,” she said at the event on Thursday.

The organization laid out its policy agenda, including plans to challenge state-level immunization requirements for school attendance, to recruit younger people to the aging organization, and to combat the installation of cell phone towers for fears of 5G and 6G.

“Never, never surrender,” said Andrew Wakefield, a former gastroenterologist whose medical license was revoked after he was found to have fabricated research indicating a link between vaccines and autism.

Recent polling suggests that one-quarter of Americans now have doubts about the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccines following a years-long campaign against immunizations by once-fringe actors. But the majority of Americans also disapprove of the Trump administration’s handling of the widening measles outbreak, which killed three people in Texas and Arizona last year and four people in Pennsylvania recently.

Being called the “largest anti-vaccine conference, probably in the world” is “a red badge of courage,” said Sen. Ron Johnson, a Republican from Wisconsin. Johnson and Sen. Rand Paul, a Republican from Kentucky, rehashed grievances over the Covid pandemic and the immunizations that were rapidly deployed to stem the tide of illness and death.

Paul repeated incorrect statements that only elderly people died from Covid, but he also suggested that deaths among those who were “thin and healthy” may have been attributed to genetic factors, proposing genetic testing to determine vulnerabilities. “There probably is in all likelihood some genotype that predisposes you to this,” Paul theorized. “If you could go in and figure out a genetic test -- those are the things we should be looking for.”

Anti-vaccine activists became nervous earlier this year after the White House reportedly put the kibosh on speaking about vaccines before the US midterm elections. “February, March, April, May, vaccine reform got a little quiet, a little scary. You know, behind the scenes, we’re like, “Yeah, what happened?” said Michael Kane, CHD’s director of advocacy. He praised Rand Paul for bringing the anti-vaccine conversation back to the national stage.

Kane urged attendees to comment on the proposed HHS changes to the way it recommends vaccines, which experts say could sow confusion and chaos. “As we’re turning the corner and looking at the midterm elections, and this is now top priority -- I mean, sometimes I gotta pinch myself,” Kane said. “Just a few years ago, we were the, you know, hated stepchild in the corner... Now we are a national movement that isn’t going anywhere.”

text:
New data from a data clearinghouse at Syracuse University reveals just how many undocumented immigrants do not have an attorney when going through cases.

In fiscal year 2021, the likelihood of having an immigration attorney present was 63%, and in 2026, it's 32%, according to Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, or TRAC.

Immigration attorney Kim Bruno said immigration cases are civil matters; therefore, you don't have the right to a government-appointed attorney as you do in criminal proceedings.

"So when we look at the right to an attorney in civil matters, do you have the right to an attorney?" Bruno said. "Well, you have the right to an attorney, but do you have the right to a free attorney? Do you have the right to have somebody represent you in court? No."

Bruno said the drop is also because there are not enough attorneys to meet the demand.

"It's overwhelmed and the pro bono work, right? There are only so many attorneys available to do this type of work. And when you have so many people detained, it makes it very difficult," Bruno said.

Meanwhile in Texas, numbers show about six out of every 10 people with a pending immigration court case in the state don't have an attorney.

Bruno says without representation, some cases are quickly resolved with deportation. But she says when people do have someone advocating on their behalf, it can take longer as they fight for their clients.

"We do other things now, like we're forced to file habeas cases. We're forced to get people out other ways. And we're forced to be very crafty with the way that we get people, their residency here, and how we can figure out different ways and go through every single avenue possible to be able to help somebody stay here and continue their life here," Bruno said.

text:
The White House has withdrawn the nomination of Lance Schroyer to be the next Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) director, according to a notice posted on the White House website Thursday.

The agency has not had a Senate-confirmed director since 2017. Former acting ICE Director Todd Lyons retired in May and David Venturella, a former private prisons executive, has been running the agency since then.

Schroyer, a former Oklahoma state trooper and close confidant of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, was nominated in June but faced pushback from the president's base and Democrats over what they said was his lack of qualifications for the job. His nomination had stalled in the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.

The White House did not give a reason for withdrawing Schroyer's nomination. ABC News has reached out to the White House for comment.

ICE's more than $75 billion budget is the largest of any law enforcement agency in the country.

The agency has become a focal point of the president's second-term deportation push and the Republican-controlled Congress has given the agency the resources to carry out the administration's agenda.

ICE has come under scrutiny during its push to deport those in the country illegally for what some Democrats say are heavy-handed tactics and a rush to hire candidates that weren't qualified for the job.

In nominating Schroyer in June, Trump touted his 29 years of service as a law enforcement officer in Oklahoma and said Schroyer will enforce the administration's crackdown on undocumented immigrants.

Schroyer, who served in the Marine Corps, is currently a senior adviser to Mullin, a former senator from Oklahoma. Schroyer was Mullin's pick to lead ICE, a source with knowledge of the decision told ABC News.

text:
Where plaintiffs sued a variety of defendants over alleged fraud involving the United States Immigrant Investor Program, but most of their claims were time barred or not plausible, the majority of their lawsuit was dismissed.

Background

This case stems from the United States Immigrant Investor Program, or the “EB-5 program,” which allows foreign nationals investing in American projects to obtain legal permanent residency. Plaintiffs have sued numerous defendants after their investment in a project was unsuccessful. Defendants have filed motions to dismiss.

Rescission

Plaintiffs assert that they each paid defendants American International & Immigration Law Group, or AIILG (the law firm of defendants Robert Lubin and Paul Ruby) retainers to serve as immigration counsel and/or “source of funds counsel” for EB-5 visa benefits through investment in the GBR LP project. Plaintiffs subsequently argue that the contracts signed by plaintiffs regarding retaining AIILG, paying administrative fees to defendant Mississippi Development Regional Center LLC, MDRC, and investments in the GBR project fall under Rule 1.8.”

The Supreme Court of Virginia has been clear: Rule 1.8 of Virginia’s Rules of Professional Conduct is a “rule of ethics, not a rule defining liabilities.” And the pertinent statute of limitations is also fatal to plaintiffs’ claim.

Securities Exchange Act

Defendants argue that the relevant statute of limitations requires that claims for rescission under § 29(b) to be brought within a year of when “plaintiff knew or should have known the facts that form the basis of rescission.” Therefore, because “Plaintiffs acknowledged the conflicts of interest when they signed the waivers,” which occurred no later than August 2017, this claim would be time-barred, they argue. The court agrees.

Moreover, plaintiffs have not pleaded fraud with sufficient particularity, and the count must also be dismissed for this reason. Defendants are also correct that plaintiffs failed to sufficiently plead the necessary elements of a rescission claim under § 29(b).

Fiduciary duty

The purported conflicts of interest were disclosed, seemingly in 2017, and plaintiffs waived them. Therefore, even applying a discovery rule standard, a “reasonable and prudent [person] under the particular circumstances” would have read the contract and discovered them at that time, accruing the statute of limitations and thus time-barring the complaint. The court also dismisses the count because plaintiffs’ complaint does not plausibly connect the “conflicts of interest” or other alleged breaches of duty to the damages they purportedly incurred.

Aiding and abetting

The Supreme Court of Virginia has required a valid predicate breach of fiduciary duty claim in order to sustain a claim of aiding and abetting breach of fiduciary duty. Therefore, without an underlying predicate act, and whereas it is unclear if it is even a cognizable cause of action, this count will be dismissed.

Statutory business conspiracy

The parties agree that a five-year statute of limitations applies to this claim. This right of action “accrues when any damage, however slight, is sustained.” As alleged in the complaint, plaintiffs’ injuries arose as early as August 2016, when plaintiffs allege they began investing in GBR and paying retainers for immigration law services to AIILG, which would mean the statute of limitations expired years ago.

Civil conspiracy

Plaintiffs premise this claim on the claims for rescission, securities fraud and breach of fiduciary duty, each of which this court has already dismissed for failing to state a claim and/or being time barred. Because the underlying torts have been dismissed, this claim is dismissed.

VCPA

This count is dismissed for failing to plead with the requisite particularity that the VCPA demands.

Legal malpractice

Because the representation before United States Citizenship and Immigration Services, or USCIS, was ongoing until the denial of the EB-5 applications, this court finds that plaintiffs have sufficiently pleaded facts that it is plausible that this action is not time-barred. Despite this, the court finds that plaintiffs have not plausibly stated a claim for legal malpractice based on conflicts of interest.

Turning to plaintiffs’ allegation that AIILG and Lubin “failed to counsel Plaintiffs” appropriately “as to the use of money exchange services in Vietnam that they knew or should have known would not meet muster with the ‘source of funds’ review of I-526 petitions sent to USCIS,” this court finds plaintiffs have plausibly alleged a legal malpractice claim with respect to these allegations.

Money had and received

Plaintiffs appear to have two theories underlying how the money was retained without right: “irreconcilable conflicts of interest” and fraud. The purported conflicts of interest cannot plausibly be a basis for this count. So too with fraud. Therefore this count is dismissed.

Accounting

Plaintiffs make solely conclusory allegations of “mismanagement” and “false assurances” that are undercut by their own factual assertions—including that the COVID-19 pandemic created “revenue challenges” and documents stating that the project is “at risk.” Therefore, this count is dismissed. And plaintiffs’ request for a receiver to be appointed is denied because there is no “proof of insolvency, fraud, waste, or improper conduct.”

Defendants’ motions to dismiss granted in part, denied in part. Hong v. Mississippi Development Regional Center, LLC, Case No. 1:25-cv-1216, Sept. 3, 2026. EDVA at Alexandria (Alston). VLW 026-3-373. 33 pp.

text:
Luz Michelle Colón, director of people and programs with IAJE, spoke on behalf of the coalition, emphasizing that individuals held inside the facility must be treated with basic human dignity. She noted that immigrant families across Mississippi are living in constant anxiety amid heightened enforcement activities.

“There is a real fear that is rampant throughout Mississippi amongst the immigrant community. You have people who are not going to work, folks afraid to go to the doctor,” Colón said. “The immigrant community in Mississippi is afraid to live, to exist, for fear of being accosted by law enforcement. This is something that is impacting all of Mississippi. They’re having to be there and exist in inhumane conditions. And it’s just not right.”

Heather Alambarrio’s husband, Jose Raphael Alambarrio, has been held at the Adams County facility since March. He was detained during a routine check-in while awaiting proceedings on an asylum application submitted after fleeing Venezuela. Heather Alambarrio recently attended a vigil outside the facility grounds.

“When I told him there were people outside holding a vigil, it really touched his heart and brought tears to his eyes because sometimes on the inside, they feel forgotten,” she said. “And they feel like people hate them or they feel invisible.”

Alambarrio, a schoolteacher in Texas, described the severe emotional and financial strain of managing household expenses alone while her husband is detained nearly seven hours away.

“There was one unit where it was over a week, and they had participated in a protest about the conditions and they were not allowed to call their significant others for a week as a consequence,” she said.

CoreCivic, the private prison operator managing the facility, and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) have disputed several of the claims. Representatives stated that allegations of inadequate medical care, unaddressed gas leaks, and tuberculosis outbreaks are unfounded, adding that full operations resumed Aug. 24 following an external incident.

In a statement to MPB, an ICE representative said a fire involving an exterior natural gas storage unit occurred outside the facility Aug. 22. The agency reported no injuries and stated operations normalized two days later.

An ICE spokesperson added: “Being in detention is a choice. We encourage all illegal aliens to take control of their departure with the CBP Home App. The United States is offering illegal aliens $3,000 and a free flight to self-deport now. We encourage every person here illegally to take advantage of this offer and reserve the chance to come back to the U.S. the right legal way to live the American dream. If not, you will be arrested and deported without a chance to return.”

Colón pushed back against the agency’s characterization.

“We would like to say that the Nuestro Coalition vehemently opposes comments that suggest ‘being in the detention center is a choice,’” Colón said. “This is not a choice for those subjected to immigration detention. The consequences are imposed by government authority and can profoundly affect individuals and their families.”

Steve Owen, a spokesperson for CoreCivic, said the facility remains fully staffed and operates in accordance with its Human Rights Policy.

In a written statement, Owen said:

“This allegation is false. While several detainees thought they may have smelled something related to a natural gas leak, none of our staff members detected anything along these lines. Out of an abundance of caution, an on-call facility maintenance staff member came in to assess the facility for any possible gas leaks, and none were found.”

Owen added: “There are no cases of tuberculosis (TB) at ACCC, nor has anyone been refused medical treatment. We are committed to providing safe, humane and respectful care for everyone entrusted to us. We take seriously our obligation to adhere to all applicable federal detention standards and will continue to ensure that all detainees receive appropriate and timely medical attention, whether as a direct provider of health services or in coordination with ICE’s Health Services Corp (IHSC) in facilities where they provide medical care.”

Advocates are calling on elected officials to conduct unsupervised visits of the facility and demanding increased transparency from CoreCivic regarding operational standards.

“Every person deserves dignity, due process, and humane treatment,” Colón said.

text:
MINNEAPOLIS (AP) — A federal immigration officer charged with shooting a Venezuelan man during the immigration crackdown that roiled Minneapolis early this year made a brief first appearance Thursday before a Minnesota judge, following months of legal and political battles over whether he would be extradited from Texas to face state charges.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer Christian Castro, handcuffed and dressed in an orange jumpsuit, stood quietly in a glass enclosure in a Minneapolis jail courtroom for the hearing. He faces a separate hearing Friday in federal court for charges that he lied to investigators about the January shooting.

Judge Paul Scoggin set bail at $400,000, or $200,000 if Castro agreed to a series of conditions, including that he sign a waiver saying he wouldn’t fight extradition back to Minnesota if he leaves the state while out on bail.

Castro, 52, signed the waiver during the hearing but was still listed as a county jail prisoner late Thursday afternoon.

He was arrested Wednesday in downtown Minneapolis by officers with the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension on state charges of assault and false reporting of a crime stemming from the shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis.

Castro’s attorney, Daniel Gerdts, declined to comment after the hearing.

Christian Castro’s arrest happened months after Minnesota charged him

In both the federal and state cases against Castro, prosecutors say he shot 24-year-old Sosa-Celis in the leg while firing through the front door of a Minneapolis home. They say Castro later falsely reported that he had been attacked with a broom handle and a snow shovel before firing his gun.

Minnesota prosecutors charged him in May but were thwarted in their efforts to bring him from his home state of Texas, where he had been arrested.

In the end, Castro came to Minnesota on his own to face federal charges in an indictment announced early this month.

“Castro invented a story to justify shooting through a front door into a house with multiple people in it,” Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, the prosecutor handling the state case, told reporters after Thursday’s hearing. “His appearance in a Hennepin County courtroom today is a critical step in our efforts to hold him accountable for that shooting.”

Friday’s hearing, in U.S. District Court in St. Paul, involves the separate federal case in which he is charged with making false statements to investigators regarding the shooting. Castro’s defense attorneys in that case have said he plans to plead not guilty.

It’s the first Justice Department prosecution of a federal officer for actions taken during this year’s massive Operation Metro Surge, which brought thousands of agents to the Twin Cities and led to sweeping protests, arrests and the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens by federal officers.

The Trump administration says only federal authorities have jurisdiction

Minnesota authorities have battled President Donald Trump’s administration over who should handle any charges against Castro. The Department of Homeland Security has called Minnesota’s prosecution of Castro “unlawful and nothing more than a political stunt,” saying only federal authorities have jurisdiction.

Authorities, including Minnesota’s Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, arrested Castro in Cameron County, Texas, on May 29, after a Minnesota judge issued a nationwide warrant. Under Texas law, Castro could be detained for 90 days, during which Minnesota sought his extradition. But Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott last month refused to sign an extradition warrant.

Castro was then released in Texas and soon after was indicted on the federal charges. He then turned himself in to federal authorities and returned to Minnesota on his own.

___

This story has been updated to correct the spelling of Sosa-Celis’ middle name and the location of Friday’s federal court hearing.

___

Bynum reported from Savannah, Georgia.
