text:
Media Matters analyzed every Fox News segment about ICE actions from June 1 through September 13, 2026. Of the 113 segments about ICE actions, only 3 acknowledged that ICE is primarily targeting immigrants with no criminal record.

Of those 3 segments, 2 came from The Story With Martha MacCallum, with the mentions of noncriminal immigrant arrests coming from Democratic guests running for Congress. The third segment appeared on America's Newsroom when Fox’s Bill Melugin mentioned “ICE’s detractors,” who pointed out that the majority of arrestees were noncriminals; Melugin then teed up ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations Acting Assistant Director Patricia Hyde to declare, “If you’re in the country illegally, you are a criminal.”

Out of Fox News' 113 segments about ICE actions, 69% (78 total) suggested that ICE actions were primarily targeting immigrants with criminal records or highlighted specific immigrants with prior convictions.

Of those 78 segments, 57 went a step further by suggesting that the immigrants being targeted by ICE were primarily violent criminals who threatened public safety.

The network's flagship morning show, Fox & Friends, led all shows, with 15 segments about ICE actions, including 12 suggesting that ICE’s targets were primarily immigrants with criminal histories. Of those 12 segments, 9 suggested that ICE targeted primarily violent criminal offenders. Meanwhile, none of the segments acknowledged that the majority of immigrants arrested by ICE had no criminal record.

As the network largely ignored the noncriminal arrest data, it also regularly fearmongered about individual immigrants accused of violent crimes, often displaying mugshots and listing out alleged offenses.

Despite a recent analysis of federal data showing that only 3% of individuals detained by ICE have a violent felony conviction, Fox News' “news-side” programming often misleadingly suggested that ICE was targeting primarily violent criminals in its immigration actions.

Fox’s “news-side” programs Fox News @ Night (6 segments), The Faulkner Focus (4), and America Reports (4) were among the leaders in suggesting that the majority of ICE actions primarily targeted violent criminals. Even on Special Report With Bret Baier — often touted as the network's flagship “straight-news” program — 3 of the program's 7 segments about ICE actions suggested that ICE was primarily targeting violent criminal immigrants.

Further, a majority of correspondent segments (15 of 26), typically presented as “straight-news” segments, pushed the narrative that ICE was primarily targeting violent criminal immigrants.

Media Matters searched transcripts in the SnapStream video database for all original programming on Fox News Channel for any of the terms “Immigration and Customs Enforcement,” “ICE,” “Department of Homeland Security,” “Homeland Security,” “Noem,” “Homan,” “Lyons,” or “DHS” within close proximity of any of the terms “alien,” “illegal,” “undocumented,” or any variations of any of the terms “migrant,” “immigrant,” “convict,” “felon,” or “criminal” and also within close proximity of any of the terms “raid,” “round up,” or “detention” or any variations of any of the terms “detain,” “deport,” or “arrest” from June 1, 2026, through September 13, 2026.

We included segments, which we defined as instances when Immigration and Customs Enforcement raids, arrests, or deportations of immigrants were the stated topic of discussion or when we found significant discussion of such ICE actions. We defined significant discussion as instances when two or more speakers in a multitopic segment discussed any such ICE actions with one another

We then reviewed the identified segments for whether they included any of the following misrepresentations of the ICE data:

Suggesting that ICE raids, arrests, or deportations are primarily targeting immigrants with prior criminal convictions or charges or immigrants newscasters describe as having prior criminal convictions or charges.

Highlighting specific immigrants with prior criminal charges or convictions or immigrants newscasters describe as having prior criminal convictions or charges in segments about ICE raids, arrests, or deportations of immigrants.

If the segment included speech that met the above criteria, analysts also reviewed those segments for whether any speaker identified the criminal conviction or charge as violent (murder, rape, larceny, or assault).

Finally, we reviewed segments for whether they identified or provided context that:

Suggested that ICE raids, arrests, or deportations are primarily targeting noncriminal immigrants or immigrants newscasters describe as not having prior criminal convictions or charges.

Highlighted specific immigrants without prior criminal charges or convictions or immigrants newscasters describe as not having prior criminal convictions or charges in segments about ICE raids, arrests, or deportations of immigrants.

description:

text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

A bill that is close to becoming law would deepen the involvement of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in combating retail crime. If it does, it would come at a time when federal crime-fighting agents are being diverted to support mass deportations, and as the public grows increasingly wary — even intolerant — of ICE’s tactics.

A Senate vote on the Combating Organized Retail Crime Act, known as CORCA, is expected by the end of the year, after passage in the House of Representatives in May. The bill, a top goal of retail industry lobbyists for years, has bipartisan support in both houses of Congress. It would create a new bureaucracy at the Department of Homeland Security — the Supply Chain Crime Coordination Center — within the Homeland Security Investigations unit.

ICE’s director would appoint the head of the new center.

Many retailers and loss prevention experts support CORCA because it streamlines cooperation between local, state and federal law enforcement and the private sector, with the goal of fighting crime. But some experts, including people in retail, loss prevention, immigration law and civil rights law, warn that it puts retailers in the middle of an immigration crackdown that has little to do with theft.

Industry groups are not focused on these concerns. In their answers to queries from Retail Dive, the National Retail Federation and the Retail Industry Leaders Association, both top CORCA boosters, sidestepped questions about ICE’s role and the diversion of HSI resources to immigration enforcement. The ICSC, which represents shopping centers, didn’t respond.

David Johnston, the NRF’s vice president of asset protection and retail operations, has testified in favor of the legislation, including earlier versions from previous Congressional sessions that didn’t get a floor vote. In an emailed statement, Johnston said that “CORCA, as written, defines the narrow scope of criminal activity involving organized retail crime and provides congressional oversight of the proposed Center under HSI.”

Problems old and new

But some experts say it’s impossible to define the scope, narrowly or otherwise, because the law doesn’t spell out exactly what these crimes legally entail and their impact has never been measured. In fact, the NRF stopped publishing its assessment of the impact in 2023, following Retail Dive’s discovery that the group had conflated two outdated survey-based shrink estimates from different years, which both factored in inventory losses unrelated to any crime.

Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Retail Dive free daily newsletter

“I see people talk about organized retail theft, but we have really not a lot of strong understanding of what’s driving it and the scope of the problem, and whether or not the actual problem is getting bigger,” said Jeff Asher, a crime analyst and co-founder of AH Datalytics. “It’s all about resource allocation, understanding the scope of the problem, and evaluating the impact of your policies. And you can’t do any of that without a strong data foundation.”

“Through this, retailers are going to be deputized to help ICE.”

Jina John

Senior Policy Counsel for AI, Privacy, and Technology, American Civil Liberties Union

One flaw of CORCA is that it lumps together cargo theft and retail theft, even though it’s unclear how related those crimes or their perpetrators actually are, he said. Another is the engagement of HSI and ICE.

“I don’t know why ICE would be involved in this to begin with,” Asher said by phone. “It seems like we’ve taken a homeland security approach to a problem that isn’t particularly well defined, and I think that’s problematic.”

HSI agents and ICE are already employed in fighting organized retail crime, but the entity created by CORCA would be able to coordinate data across federal, state, local and tribal law enforcement and private entities in an unprecedented way, according to Jina John, senior policy counsel for AI, Privacy, and Technology at the American Civil Liberties Union.

“Through this, retailers are going to be deputized to help ICE,” she said by video conference.

Diverting resources

If CORCA passes, a new crime hub would be established at a time when DHS is increasingly redirecting resources and personnel to immigration enforcement, according to research from the Cato Institute, a libertarian think tank.

Read More in Operations

Last year, nearly 90% of HSI agents — 6,198 out of 7,100 — were diverted to support ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations, according to the report. HSI, whose media contact is at ICE, didn’t immediately respond to emailed questions about CORCA and Cato’s findings.

“I would imagine that many retailers, small or large, don’t want their stores becoming a locus for racial profiling and aggressive immigration enforcement actions.”

Heidi Altman

Vice President of Policy, National Immigration Law Center

“HSI’s role, which is part of ICE, has really expanded. It has gone from looking at transnational crimes and national security issues to what we’ve seen in the past year and a half — that, at times, it’s been almost exclusively about immigration enforcement,” the ACLU’s John said. “Not entirely, but almost exclusively. And we’ve seen those abuses.”

The public has increasingly turned against ICE, with over half of Americans saying they have little to no confidence in the agency, according to a poll from YouGov taken in July, after ICE agents killed people in Texas and Maine. Half are in favor of abolishing ICE, according to that report. Nearly 60% agree that ICE surges in places like Minnesota make communities less safe, according to a poll from PRRI, a nonpartisan think tank that researches religion, culture and public policy.

HSI is no longer “firewalled from civil immigration enforcement,” according to Heidi Altman, vice president of policy at the National Immigration Law Center.

“I would imagine that many retailers, small or large, don’t want their stores becoming a locus for racial profiling and aggressive immigration enforcement actions,” she said by phone. “You have this retail-crime enforcement mechanism that is within ICE, plunged into communities and working directly with retailers.”

Read More in Operations

Evan Armstrong, senior vice president of government affairs at RILA, said in a statement that “CORCA does not give ICE new immigration-enforcement powers or turn organized retail crime enforcement into an immigration function.” He didn’t respond to follow-up questions about Cato’s report and the Trump administration’s directive to employ existing agents and resources for immigration enforcement.

The NRF didn’t respond directly to questions about these issues, except to say that Congress could tackle them after the bill becomes law. Retail Dive reached out to several co-sponsors of the bill in both the House and Senate, including 10 Democrats who reportedly pulled their support, but none have responded.

Consequences for retailers

In advocating for CORCA, industry groups, law enforcement and asset protection professionals often cite safety concerns. “Organized retail and supply chain crime is a public safety issue that impacts retail and supply chain workers, consumers and communities nationwide,” NRF’s Johnston told Retail Dive.

But lawyers specialized in immigration and due process warn that stores could become the nexus of disruptive and even violent encounters with federal agents, along with data collection that could entangle everyday shoppers. Some within the retail industry and loss prevention field share such concerns.

“This disproportionately affects lower income and minority groups.”

Nick Egelanian

President, SiteWorks

Nick Egelanian, president of retail development firm SiteWorks, said that CORCA is likely to have “many unintended negative consequences” that retailers and retail property owners should want no part of.

text:
Tatiana and Viktor Vdovin showed up for their routine check-in meeting with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Aug. 18 as they had every year since fleeing Russia in 2022.

The Vdovins and their two children have a pending family asylum claim and are required to regularly meet with ICE officers until their court date.

The meetings typically unfold without much intrigue: The family heads back to the office together, goes over paperwork and returns to their home in Indian Trail, a suburban town in Union County just outside Charlotte city limits, until their next appointment.

Something was off this time. Officials in the Charlotte ICE office called Viktor first. Just Viktor.

When they called Tatiana some time later, her husband was gone.

ICE detained Viktor and sent him to the Stewart Detention Center in Georgia. They offered no explanation, telling Tatiana she would receive more information at a later time.

Outside in the hall, her kids were crying. Tatiana pleaded with the officers to take her instead. Her husband’s job paid the bills, she said. They declined.

“I asked them about the whole situation: Why him, not me. I’m the main case person, the holder of the family case. But he said nothing,” Tatiana said. “We were very scared in that moment because we don’t know what we should do.”

Tatiana was paralyzed by the weight of the situation, she said, unable to think or do much of anything. The stakes were enormous.

Her family cannot safely return to their home country, where they opposed the war and the current government. That’s why they applied for asylum in the United States in the first place.

Beyond fears for their well-being, the threat of deportation was a shock because they thought they were authorized to stay in the country, Tatiana said. The Vdovins received a letter from U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services in May stating as much. “You may remain in the United States until your asylum application is decided,” it read. USCIS is the federal agency that processes immigration applications.

But the letter’s assurance holds little weight with ICE. Even for a family like the Vdovins, who entered the country at an official port of entry and followed the lawful asylum process, a pending case is more a state of limbo than a guarantee of security: They don’t have unlawful presence, but they don’t have lawful status, either.

They’re stuck in a yearslong waiting period until a backlogged court system hears their case. The family’s immigration court hearing is scheduled for November 2027, but Viktor’s case was separated from the rest of his family after getting detained. His master calendar hearing is Thursday.

Under previous administrations — including President Donald Trump’s first term — ICE officials didn’t ordinarily arrest people under these circumstances, said Mary Lynn Tedesco, a Charlotte-based immigration attorney. Tedesco does not represent the Vdovins and did not speak to their specific case.

But Trump’s mass deportation campaign continues to push beyond its purported focus on violent criminals and what the White House calls “the worst of the worst.”

USCIS and ICE are both arms of the Department of Homeland Security. Now, while one branch of DHS tells families they can stay if they follow the rules, the other is increasingly arresting them for doing just that.

“They’re reporting as they are supposed to, as they’ve been told to for their cases, and ICE is detaining people just because their case is still pending,” Tedesco said. “One of the main things that I’ve heard people say to me is, ‘I don’t understand. They were doing everything the right way.’ And it’s like, I know, but unfortunately right now that doesn’t necessarily matter.”

In a statement provided by an ICE spokesperson, the agency said the United States granted Viktor a limited parole period in the United States when he entered the country. That period ended by the time of Viktor’s scheduled check-in meeting, and the court had not yet heard his case, according to ICE.

“Any application pending before (immigration) does not, by itself, confer lawful immigration status or preclude detention during pending immigration proceedings,” the statement reads. “Vdovin will have the opportunity to present his claims before an immigration judge.”

ICE arrests reach new highs with boost from non-criminals

Before last year, Tedesco only went to court about once every other month. She worked closely with DHS attorneys to determine which cases were worth spending court resources and taxpayer dollars on. The department prioritized people with criminal records or fraud issues, Tedesco said.

DHS severed communication in 2025. Now Tedesco is in court three to four times a week at emergency hearings for clients whom she’d never before seen targeted for removal.

Viktor is among tens of thousands of other immigrants who were detained this summer despite maintaining a clean record, reporting from The New York Times shows.

The number of arrests ballooned after ICE set an ambitious goal of 2,000 per day. That has driven up detentions for people with pending asylum claims and green card holders with minor infractions to their names.

The agency recorded nearly 50,000 arrests in July, a record for Trump’s second term. Less than 4% of those cases involved a person with a past violent criminal conviction, The New York Times reported. A majority of cases involved people with no criminal history at all.

That’s a significant departure from previous administrations, Tedesco said.

“If you were doing what you were supposed to do, generally speaking, the rule was that ICE was not going to bother to detain you,” Tedesco said. “Now we have people that show up in the Charlotte ICE office, for example, and they have filed their asylum applications … ICE is arresting those people, too. And so that’s where I’m seeing my major uptick.”

“That’s the part that’s jarring to me and my practice.”

‘Model neighbor’ waits for court ruling from detention

Tatiana received her first call from Viktor about five hours after his arrest. It was only a minute and played out over speaker phone.

“He said he is OK, and that I need to solve something to have money because he’s thinking about the bond for his freedom. And that’s all. Our connection is stopped,” she recalled.

He called again the next day, this time for two minutes, and asked her to find an attorney. She found one through a Russian-speaking friend who had faced a similar situation in May, she said. Their friend was ultimately freed on a $20,000 bond.

Viktor has been locked away from his family for a month with no end in sight. One day before his Sept. 2 bond hearing, the federal government filed a motion to dismiss his habeas corpus petition, which is what allowed him to seek bond. Viktor’s attorneys responded with their own motion challenging the government, and now they are waiting for the federal judge to make a decision.

It’s unclear how long that process could take. Tatiana is in contact with two other Russian-speaking families who have been waiting on a decision for about four months and counting, she said.

Tatiana and Viktor Vdovin have been together for almost 20 years. Their 15th wedding anniversary came and went with Viktor in detention.

“What I love most about him is probably his kindness, his loyalty to the people he loves and the way he takes care of our family,” Tatiana said. “He is my best friend and the person I have built my whole adult life with.”

Viktor has been a hard worker since 13, when he took his first job to help his family. Lately, he’s been saving up to buy a house. Tatiana doesn’t know if that will be possible after paying attorney fees and a bond amount that’s likely to reach five figures.

Tatiana, once a pastry chef in Russia, works as a cake designer at Harris Teeter. Viktor started a remodeling business that provides tiling services. They love spending as much time as they can with their 13-year-old daughter, Varvara, and their 10-year-old son, Matvei, when they’re all together.

“In my view, this is a crime,” said Leigh Coulter, the Vdovins’ neighbor. “(Viktor) is here on asylum. He has no criminal record. Model neighbors. Good job. Clients. Kids in school. The whole thing.”

Coulter has tried to raise awareness about their case and get Viktor freed, making calls to the state attorney general’s office and to North Carolina members of Congress. She hasn’t made much headway, she said.

Viktor’s first days in detention were especially difficult. He was exhausted but couldn’t eat due to the stress he was under, Tatiana said. He’s warehoused in a facility with well over 1,000 people, many of whom are sick or sleep on the floor, Tatiana said. Viktor got sick with something, too.

But he’s been able to connect with his family over paid FaceTime calls, which have lifted everybody’s spirits. Now, all they can do is wait for the courts to act.

“I hope that it will be soon,” Tatiana Vdovin said. “And that’s the only thing I can hold everything up on. I’m just hopeful, that’s all.”

text:
On September 14, 2026, a federal judge in Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration v. Department of Homeland Security issued a preliminary injunction preventing a U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) final rule that would have ended the longstanding “duration of status” framework and replaced it with fixed admission periods for F-1 international students, J-1 exchange visitors, and I foreign media representatives from taking effect as scheduled on September 15, 2026.

Quick Hits

On July 17, 2026, DHS published a final rule—scheduled to take effect on September 15, 2026—that would end the longstanding duration of status framework for F, J, and I visa holders.

A U.S. district court found that the government’s national security justification for the rule was arbitrary and capricious.

The duration of status framework remains in effect as litigation continues.

On July 17, 2026, DHS published a final rule scheduled to take effect on September 15, 2026, that would replace the duration of status (D/S) admission framework for F, J, and I nonimmigrants with fixed periods of admission. The rule also shortened the departure grace period for F and J visa holders from sixty days to thirty days and imposed a modified unlawful presence framework—one based on failure to timely file an extension-of-stay application rather than a formal U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) finding of a status violation or an immigration judge’s removal order. Additionally, the rule imposed certain restrictions on F-1 students’ ability to transfer schools or change academic programs.

On August 18, 2026, a coalition of plaintiffs led by the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration filed a complaint and motion for preliminary injunction in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts challenging DHS’s final rule. The complaint argued that DHS violated the Administrative Procedure Act, provided an inadequate public comment period, and exceeded its statutory authority. The plaintiffs contended that the changes would create significant uncertainty and administrative burdens for impacted individuals and institutions. On the eve of the rule’s effective date, the district judge in Presidents’ Alliance v. DHS granted nationwide preliminary relief, finding that DHS’s stated justifications were arbitrary and capricious and that allowing the rule to take effect would cause immediate and irreparable harm.

Next Steps

For now, F, J, and I visa holders do not need to apply for extensions of stay with USCIS and those traveling to the United States will continue to be admitted in D/S status. Employers and foreign nationals should remain vigilant and may want to be prepared for a possible reversal while the litigation continues.

An ICE agent charged in a Minneapolis shooting and held in a Texas jail for months is now booked in Hennepin County Jail ahead of a possible hearing later this week.

According to the Hennepin County Attorney’s Office, ICE agent Christian Castro was arrested on Wednesday by the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension on state charges.

As previously reported, Castro is accused of shooting at Julio Sosa-Celis through the door of a north Minneapolis home on Jan. 14 in the course of his duties as a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer during Operation Metro Surge.

He had initially told FBI investigators that Sosa-Celis and others had attacked him, using a snow shovel and a broom handle as weapons. Video evidence of the shooting contradicted his sworn statement, and Castro was placed on leave as the U.S. Department of Justice investigated whether he lied under oath.

Castro was charged in Hennepin County earlier this year with four felony counts of second-degree assault with a dangerous weapon and one misdemeanor count of falsely reporting a crime.

RELATED: ICE agent charged in non-fatal shooting of Venezuelan man

He was released in late August from the Brownsville jail in Texas after the 90-day limit on his detention expired under state law. DHS said Castro remains suspended without pay while the investigation continues.

On Sept. 4, Castro made his initial court appearance on separate federal charges that accused him of lying about the shooting.

RELATED: ICE agent makes initial court appearance for Minneapolis shooting, indictment unsealed

Castro could make his first appearance on Thursday afternoon in Hennepin County.

Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty released the following statement, in part:

“Gov. Abbott’s attempt to shield Mr. Castro from accountability has failed. We look forward to commencing our prosecution.”

text:
A mother is demanding answers after her teenage son was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents in Alamo and a video of the encounter went viral on social media.

The incident happened on Sept. 11 on Alamo Road near the expressway. The video shows part of a confrontation between ICE agents and two 17-year-olds.

In the video, a red car is stopped in the middle of the road. Two people appear to try to pull the passenger out of the car.

The teen is pulled out and placed on the ground as two ICE agents hold him down while trying to handcuff him. Moments later, another teen gets out of the driver's seat and is seen frantically looking around.

The video then shows one of the ICE agents hit the other teen in the face four times with her hand.

Luis Ochoa was driving the red car. He says he and his friend are both American citizens and were on their way to a Marine recruiter's office when it happened.

"We saw an ICE raid on a truck. We stopped to record, and when we were recording, my friend JC gets smacked by one of the agents," Ochoa said.

"The woman hits him with the door, and that's when everything starts. The woman chases him back to my car. Once inside my car, she put [her] elbow on his neck and I was like, 'Miss please stop. He's a minor. Don't treat him like that,'" Ochoa said.

Ochoa says he was then pepper-sprayed and taken into custody.

"[They] arrested me for no reason. They got on top of me saying, 'Don't resist.' I was never resisting. They broke my wrist," Ochoa said.

His mother, Teresa Ochoa, says watching the video is hard.

"He is a minor; it's traumatic enough for an adult — for something like this to happen to him is really tough," Teresa Ochoa said. "It was eight hours without hearing from him; they wouldn't give me any information — they behaved very badly."

Channel 5 News reached out to the Department of Homeland Security. DHS has a different account of what happened.

DHS described the teens as "anti-ICE" agitators and says they were arrested after trying to obstruct officers during a vehicle stop. The agency says one of the teens banged repeatedly on an ICE vehicle window and refused orders to stop.

DHS says he then became verbally and physically combative when officers tried to detain him. The agency says officers used the minimum force necessary and relied on de-escalation and use-of-force training.

DHS also says two ICE officers suffered minor injuries and were treated at a local clinic.

See the full statement from DHS below:

“On September 11, 2026, ICE officers arrested two anti-ICE agitators after they attempted to obstruct officers conducting a vehicle stop in Alamo, Texas. The two agitators proceeded to follow the officers once they returned to their vehicle, and one of the individuals approached the government vehicle and repeatedly banged on the officer’s window. Officers verbally commanded the agitator to stop his actions, but he refused. When officers exited the vehicle and attempted to detain him, the agitator became verbally and physically combative and resisted officers. Officers relied on their training to control the situation, and the agitators were placed under arrest. Deportation officers sustained minor injuries and were treated at a local clinic.

"Violence against ICE officers, or any law enforcement personnel, will not be tolerated. Our officers carry out their Congressionally mandated duties in service to public safety and the rule of law. Any bystander or individual who assaults, obstructs, or violently attacks officers will be subject to arrest and prosecution permitted by law.

“ICE law enforcement officers are trained to use the minimum amount of force necessary to resolve dangerous situations to prioritize the safety of the public and our officers. Officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics and regularly receive ongoing use of force training.

“ICE is not going to schools to make arrests. If a dangerous or violent illegal criminal alien felon were to flee into a daycare, or a child sex offender is working as an employee, there may be a situation where an arrest is made to protect the safety of the children.”

Teresa Ochoa disagrees with that account.

"Justice must be served — and it must be served against the officers who beat them," Teresa Ochoa said.

The teens filed a police report with the Alamo Police Department. An Alamo police spokesperson said the department is forwarding the case to the DHS Office of Inspector General, an independent watchdog that investigates issues within DHS.

Watch the video above for the full story.

title: DHS explains how it identified potential noncitizen voters, plans to provide list to Pa.
authors: Carter Walker, VoteBeat, Carter Walker, Whitney Downard
description:
When DHS first informed Pennsylvania about the potential noncitizen registered voters in July, it told the Pennsylvania Department of State that Social Security numbers had been used in some of the matches.
However, this led to confusion given that Pennsylvania has not provided the Trump administration with a list of registered voters that includes Social Security numbers.
The email also said that some of the 14,576 registered voters it flagged in Pennsylvania were firmer matches than others.
In the email, DHS said it would send Pennsylvania officials a list of the potential noncitizens it identified.

text:
This article was originally published by Votebeat, a nonprofit news organization covering local election administration and voting access.

New records provide the most detail so far about the previously opaque process by which the federal government concluded that thousands of potential noncitizens are registered to vote in Pennsylvania.

On July 16, the day President Donald Trump delivered a high-profile speech on election security, the Department of Homeland Security said it had found more than 250,000 potential noncitizens registered to vote in California, Nevada, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania. The states, though, called into question the accuracy of that number and asked for more information on how it was calculated.

DHS answered Pennsylvania’s query on Sept. 9, according to an email to Secretary of the Commonwealth Al Schmidt obtained by Votebeat and Spotlight PA. The department said the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’ Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate identified the potential noncitizens by comparing the state’s publicly available voter roll to internal DHS databases.

The email broke nearly two months of silence from the Trump administration over exactly how it arrived at the numbers Trump referenced in his July speech.

When DHS first informed Pennsylvania about the potential noncitizen registered voters in July, it told the Pennsylvania Department of State that Social Security numbers had been used in some of the matches. However, this led to confusion given that Pennsylvania has not provided the Trump administration with a list of registered voters that includes Social Security numbers.

But the Sept. 9 email, signed only by the DHS Office of Intergovernmental Affairs, said that DHS had not used “federal enumerators” like Social Security numbers to perform the matching. Instead, it said it used fields such as first name, last name, date of birth, phone number, and address.

DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the conflicting information.

The email also said that some of the 14,576 registered voters it flagged in Pennsylvania were firmer matches than others. “The more attributes from the individual registered voter that match an individual in DHS immigration records, the higher the confidence level of the match,” the email said.

“The highest confidence level of matching indicators, for example, first name, last name, middle name, date of birth, address, and phone number would be a 6-attribute match. If an individual did not have the same phone number or the same address, this would be a lower confidence match but likely still the same individual.”

The email went on to say that if matches were not made on all six main criteria, other indicators may have been used, such as previous addresses or spousal information.

In the email, DHS said it would send Pennsylvania officials a list of the potential noncitizens it identified. “Each one of the 14,576 individuals identified should be carefully reviewed by your state to determine eligibility for voting in a federal election,” it wrote.

The email offered Pennsylvania the choice of sending the registered voters’ federal enumerators to DHS to confirm or deny their citizenship, or conducting its own analysis.

It’s unclear whether the department has sent Pennsylvania the list of alleged noncitizens registered to vote since sending the email last week. A spokesperson for the Pennsylvania Department of State did not respond to a question on whether the list had been provided yet.

Pennsylvania, as well as Nevada, recently called into question DHS’ confidence in its own numbers.

In Nevada, staff in the secretary of state’s office recorded an August call in which DHS officials said the original figure of potential noncitizens it had identified represented “the ceiling” of how many noncitizens were actually on the rolls.

In a letter recapping an August call with DHS representatives, Schmidt said that “DHS representatives explained that they did not have high confidence” in the figures they were presenting.

In its Sept. 9 email, the department disputed Schmidt’s framing, calling it a “blatant mischaracterization.”

A spokesperson for the Department of State said its characterization of the call was accurate, and that the state would only use “credible” information to maintain its voter rolls.

“Voters can be confident that eligible Pennsylvania citizens will not be disenfranchised by faulty methodology or unreliable data,” Matt Heckel said in an email.

description:

“Over a year ago, farm workers across Southern California endured weeks of horrific attacks targeting them because of the color of their skin.

text:
LOS ANGELES – A federal court granted a preliminary injunction in Vasquez Perdomo v. Mullin that blocks the Trump administration from continuing its unlawful practice of conducting warrantless arrests without first determining whether a person is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. The court also certified a class of individuals who, since June 6, 2025, have been or will be arrested by federal agents for alleged immigration violations, without a warrant, and without an individualized escape risk assessment.

“This ruling is one of the most important decisions to date in the community’s effort to end the federal government’s cruel and illegal practice of abducting people and separating them from their families,” said Mayra Joachin, senior staff attorney at the ACLU Foundation of Southern California. “By requiring immigration agents to follow the law’s requirement to make escape risk determinations before they can arrest someone without a warrant, this court order should put an end to hundreds–if not more–of unlawful arrests that continue throughout Southern California. We will closely monitor compliance with this court order, and expect the federal government to abide by it.”

In its order, the court found federal immigration agents are “regularly abstaining from conducting a likelihood of escape analysis at all.” Further, the court notes “plaintiffs have demonstrated that the policy is ongoing” and that the testimony by DHS’s own agents support the conclusion that it was due to this illegal warrantless arrest policy and not “isolated instances of agents going rogue.”

“⁨⁨The Trump administration jettisoned federal law in order to achieve its goal of mass deportation at any cost, disappearing Angeleno community members in a matter of moments as they go about their daily lives. Thanks in part to the sworn testimony of dozens of plaintiffs and class members who came forward to speak out about their unlawful arrests, the court rightfully recognized that DHS is violating the law as a matter of policy. We will continue fighting alongside our plaintiffs, workers and immigrant communities to ensure that everyone can go about their daily lives without fear of being arbitrarily stopped or arrested,⁩” said Lauren Michel Wilfong, National Day Laborer Organizing Network (NDLON) staff attorney.

“Over a year ago, farm workers across Southern California endured weeks of horrific attacks targeting them because of the color of their skin. This decision reaffirms that these illegal, racist raids targeting working class people should have never happened,” said United Farm Workers President Teresa Romero. “This recognition is accompanied by important legal restraints on the Trump administration’s ability to terrorize California’s immigrant workers. From downtown Los Angeles to the fields of Oxnard and Coachella, this ruling will make every worker safer.”

Under federal law, immigration agents may make a warrantless civil immigration arrest only when they have probable cause to believe both that a person is undocumented and that the person is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. In addition to stopping the unlawful practice of conducting warrantless arrests without first determining whether a person is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained, the court orders the federal government to comply with the following conditions:

immigration agents must consider totality of circumstances known to agent before making the arrest, including escape risk

agents must stop relying on the escape risk standard or analytical approach set forth in the five-page memorandum from former acting director of ICE, Todd Lyons, issued in January 2026, which illegally suggested that merely being undocumented was sufficient as a likelihood of escape

Agents must document their analysis of escape risk when conducting warrantless arrests in the Central District.

“Every worker deserves to go to work with dignity and without fear of being unlawfully detained,” said Armando Gudino, executive director of the Los Angeles Worker Center Network. “No one should have their safety or basic rights threatened simply because of where they work, the language they speak or what they look like. This ruling is an important step toward restoring that fundamental sense of security for all workers, especially immigrant workers across our various communities.”

Evidence obtained in the case showed that of a sample of 113 arrest records produced by the government in discovery, nearly 80 percent either contained no escape-risk assessment at all or relied largely on boilerplate language. Immigration authorities confirmed in sworn testimony that their practice is not to arrest individuals without independently assessing their risk of escape. As a consequence, agents routinely fail to ask people about factors relevant to whether they can be arrested, including their jobs, families, homes and other community ties.

"Today, the community feels more protected with the court's order that DHS' warrantless arrests likely violate federal law. This gives them breathing room to go about their daily lives, providing for their families while continuing to demonstrate such incredible resilience in the face of the Trump administration's ongoing attacks. We know this is but one step in the pursuit of justice, but for today, we have prevailed,” said Angelica Salas, executive director of the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights (CHIRLA), a plaintiff.

The lawsuit was originally brought by five individual Latino workers and three membership organizations—CHIRLA, LAWCN and UFW—as well as Immigrant Defenders Law Center (ImmDef), a legal services provider.

“It’s an honor to stand with our plaintiffs and co-counsel who are leading the fight to end the government’s lawless campaign of immigration raids in the courts and on the streets,” said Annie Lai, director of the Immigrant and Racial Justice Solidarity Clinic at the UC Irvine School of Law. “That fight is as urgent as ever. Even as we celebrate this court order and the courage of all those who are willing to hold the government accountable, we know there is much hard work ahead.”

The plaintiffs are represented by the ACLU SoCal; Public Counsel; Law Offices of Stacy Tolchin; UC Irvine School of Law Immigrant and Racial Justice Solidarity Clinic; NDLON; Munger, Tolles & Olson LLP; ACLU Foundations of Northern California and San Diego & Imperial Counties; Hecker Fink LLP; Martinez Aguilasocho Law, Inc; CHIRLA and ImmDef.

text:
Veteran journalist Luis Galeano, one of at least 94 Nicaraguans whom the Ortega Murillo regime has stripped of citizenship in recent years for opposing the government, has been detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Galeano, who has continued critically reporting on the Sandinista government online through his platform, Café con voz, since shortly after arriving in the US in 2018, has had an asylum application pending for about seven years, according to his wife, Daykel Santamaría. He also has a work permit and a social security number, she said.

Nonetheless, shortly after beginning his second job driving Lyft on Monday morning in Florida, ICE agents pulled him over. As of Wednesday, Galeano was detained at Krome detention center in Miami. He has an immigration court date scheduled for 2 October, Santamaría said.

“Deporting [Galeano] to Nicaragua would be a death sentence,” said Javier Melendez, a sociologist who has been friends with the journalist for more than 30 years. The Sandinista government also stripped Melendez of his citizenship; he’s now a US citizen, living in Washington DC. The denaturalization order also affected acclaimed novelist Sergio Ramírez and poet and writer Gioconda Belli.

Ice has been contacted for comment.

Melendez called the situation facing his friend “a double trauma – he escaped from his country because of his work and then the place where he sought refuge detains him due to their domestic politics”.

Galeano fled Nicaragua in December, 2018, days after police raided 100% Noticias, the outlet where he worked, and issued an order for his arrest. He arrived in Miami shortly thereafter and petitioned for asylum, according to Santamaría.

Santamaría said she didn’t know if her husband was, effectively, a man without a country due to the 2023 measure denaturalizing him as a Nicaraguan.

Meanwhile, on Tuesday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee had a two hour-plus hearing on “Confronting the Totalitarian Ortega-Murillo Regime.” Florida Rep. María Elvira Salazar, committee chairperson, opened the hearing by denouncing how Daniel Ortega and Rosa Murillo “have spent years dismantling democracy”, and warned that “the Administration is paying attention, and Ortega and Murillo should consider themselves warned.”

The disjunction between the US government locking up a journalist targeted by the Nicaraguan government for reporting on its totalitarian tendencies, while at the same time denouncing those same tendencies is an example of “the serious and profound contradictions” in the Trump administration when it comes to Nicaragua, said Ana María Méndez Dardón, Central America director at the Washington Office on Latin America.

Galeano’s detention is one example many of “how due process is missing from the right to asylum” under the Trump administration, she added.

Salazar issued a statement after Galeano’s detention saying: “America must always know the difference between a criminal and a political exile.” Queries from the Guardian to the committee and several of its members were not answered.

Galeano’s detention has also been denounced by Salazar’s GOP colleague in Florida, Rep. Mario Díaz-Balart, who posted a statement on X saying, “The United States has long been a beacon of freedom for those persecuted by tyranny. We must uphold that tradition…”

The Committee to Protect Journalists and the Inter American Press Association called for Galeano’s release.

Although Galeano escaped Nicaragua under threat of arrest in late 2018, records of him being targeted for his reporting date at least as far back as 23 Feb., 2011, when Amnesty International issued a bulletin titled, “Urgent Action,” warning that his life was in danger after “an unknown individual called [him] on his mobile phone and said ‘You have 72 hours to change your mind about what you’ll publish, otherwise your family won’t see you anymore.’”

The caller referred to Galeano’s reporting for El Nuevo Diario on government misuse of around $20m between 2004 and 2008.

Recently, the journalist had been seeing ICE agents in the streets of Miami with increasing alarm while driving Lyft. “He called me like a week ago, asking if I could help with a new journalism project he had in mind, a morning news program on the region [of Latin America],” said Melendez, who founded Expediente Abierto, a think tank on Central America.

“He wanted to get off the streets, seeing the raids everywhere,” Melendez said.

Santamaría, Galeano’s wife, said the two had spoken often about what would happen if one or the either was detained. Plans included calling their lawyer, alerting the media, trying to stay calm. “We prepared ourselves mentally for this moment,” she said.

“We’ve already lived through going into exile, having an order of arrest – these are situations that make you more mature,” she said.

Galeano spoke with his wife several times Wednesday. She described him as calm, telling her, “If God got me out of Nicaragua, he’ll get me out of here.” She said she has faith the US government will see what she called “a very well-documented asylum case”.

​​​​​​​​​​​FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE

Media Contacts

press@oag.maryland.gov

410-576-7009

BALTIMORE, MD – Attorney General Anthony G. Brown today filed an amicus brief in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland urging the court to grant a preliminary injunction blocking U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) from continuing its pattern and practice of unlawful warrantless arrests across Maryland.

The brief was filed in Guzmán v. DHS, a class action lawsuit brought by Samuel Guzmán, three other individual plaintiffs, and We Are CASA, which alleges that ICE has systematically arrested people in Maryland without a warrant and without the individualized probable cause determinations required by federal law. Federal law permits a warrantless immigration arrest only when officers have probable cause both that a person is unlawfully present in the United States and that the person is likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained.

“The law is clear about what ICE must establish before making a warrantless arrest, and Maryland families are entitled to that protection,” said Attorney General Brown. “This brief urges the court to hold ICE to the law and put a stop to unlawful arrests in our State.”

Maryland’s brief supports the plaintiffs’ request for a preliminary injunction requiring ICE to cease making warrantless immigration arrests in Maryland without a probable cause determination pre-arrest that the person will flee before a warrant can be obtained. The brief argues that ICE’s disregard of these safeguards has caused widespread harm in Maryland, contributing to declining graduation rates among Hispanic and English-learner students, immigrants avoiding medical care out of fear, disruptions to businesses and the local economy, and diminished trust in law enforcement that makes victims and witnesses less likely to report crimes or cooperate with police.

The brief further notes that ICE has purportedly arrested nearly 7,000 people in Maryland without a warrant since January 2025, a nearly 500 percent increase in the weekly rate of such arrests compared to the previous year. Those arrested have included U.S. citizens, among them Annapolis-born plaintiff Samuel Guzmán.

More than one million Marylanders are immigrants. The Attorney General is fighting to ensure that the rights of the immigrant community and the rights of all Marylanders are protected. For more information on the Attorney General’s efforts, visit the Federal Actions Response page on our website.

text:
A federal judge ruled late Tuesday that the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) may not send any more warning notices to the New York man who sent a critical email to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), saying the practice “likely” violated the First Amendment.

U.S. District Judge Rudolph Contreras, appointed by former President Obama, placed a preliminary injunction to block DHS from delivering letters appearing to threaten David Streever — who wrote a scathing email to former acting ICE Director Todd Lyons comparing the immigration official to a Nazi leader.

Streever sued DHS in July after he claimed two federal officers came to his home while he was out of the country and delivered a warning notice to his wife — which stated the man’s comments might constitute a criminal threat against federal personnel.

The email condemned the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens during immigration enforcement operations in Minneapolis, saying the actions would “lead to [Lyons’s] downfall.” Streever, a Rochester resident, also compared the then acting ICE director to Nazi Germany police official Reinhard Heydrich, often referred to as “the butcher.”

Streever sued DHS and accused the agency of unjustly retaliating against him for his criticism, violating his free speech. The lawsuit alleges DHS officials later tracked him to a New York City hotel after he returned to the country, left him repeated voicemails and sought to have him sign a warning notice.

“The notice practically shouts that Mr. Streever may be prosecuted if he continues to engage in his political speech,” the judge wrote. “Even if Defendant’s benign explanation of the notice were plausible, Mr. Streever ‘reasonably understood [the notice] to convey a threat of adverse government action,’ namely prosecution.”

Contreras wrote that the First Amendment affirms Americans’ ability to criticize officials and that Streever’s email was not a “true threat of violence” — which the Constitution does not grant the same protection.

A DHS spokesperson told The Hill in a Wednesday statement that any “allegation DHS and its components are attempting to ‘squash’ free speech is categorically FALSE.”

“ICE investigates all credible threats towards its employees and officers, including threats to the ICE Director,” the spokesperson continued, also citing increased rates of violence against immigration agents.

A senior ICE official wrote in a declaration submitted to the court that the agency has seen a “dramatic” increase in threats to its personnel since early 2025. They added its investigation into Streever’s email closed June 30.

Lawyers from the Department of Justice did not claim the message to Lyons contained any threat, according to court documents.

Contreras acknowledged the department’s concern given the rise in threats, which he called concerning, and permitted the department to investigate such threats “so long as they do not issue threats to Mr. Streever deterring protected speech, such as the Warning Notice.”

The ruling allows DHS two weeks to appeal.

text:
By RYAN J. FOLEY

The Trump administration has ordered caregivers for migrant children to stop reporting human trafficking concerns directly to the office created to help victims, a change that critics say could make some vulnerable minors easier to deport.

The directive, in a Sept. 10 memo reviewed by The Associated Press, could mean that some victims would be denied services and face tougher odds of obtaining asylum and visas allowing them to stay in the United States.

“This is going to harm children,” said Jean Bruggeman, co-executive director of Freedom Network USA, a coalition that advocates for human trafficking survivors. “This makes it more likely they will be deported before they get the services they need and put back into harm’s way.”

The order added another plank to the Trump administration’s hard-line immigration agenda that has forged the most restrictive policies toward immigrants in more than a generation. Some of those efforts have been stopped by courts but many others have taken root.

The memo said the change would “streamline the reporting, tracking and referral of trafficking-related concerns.” An administration statement said the change was an effort to reduce the high number of claims that did not rise to the level of criminal human trafficking but nonetheless triggered the award of benefits and relief.

But Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon said the change requires children and their advocates to report human trafficking to the same agency that is holding them in custody. “This move to sideline human trafficking experts is more evidence that the Trump administration will deport kids to score political points rather than actually protect them,” he said.

Office has helped thousands of trafficking victims

The change applies to 1,800 children who are in federal custody after arriving in the United States without parents or being arrested with parents who were not legally present, and others who have been released but remain under supervision.

Under longstanding policy, caregivers are required to conduct an initial screening of unaccompanied children for potential labor or sex trafficking within five days of admission to a facility or shelter. If they suspect the child is a victim, they have been required within 24 hours to notify the Office of Trafficking in Persons, which was created in 2015 to prevent human trafficking and protect victims.

If the office certifies the claim, the minors become eligible for a program that gives them greater freedom by allowing them to move out of short-term housing, placing them in foster care and allowing them to attend public school. It does not protect them from deportation immediately, but they can use the determination to pursue visas for victims of trafficking or asylum claims. It also grants eligibility for nutrition, housing and other public benefits once they are released from federal custody.

Thousands of unaccompanied minors have benefited from the office’s determinations. They are particularly susceptible to labor and sex trafficking, including in their home countries, on their way to the U.S. and after they arrive, and that’s why Congress has given them protections, Bruggeman said.

Administration says change will target improper claims

Under the change ordered last week by the administration, federal employees and care providers were told to no longer report labor and sex trafficking claims involving the minors to the Office on Trafficking in Persons.

Instead, the memo said those claims should be submitted only to the Office of Refugee Resettlement, which oversees the housing of unaccompanied minors. That office will now investigate the claims and decide which ones should be forwarded to the Office on Trafficking in Persons for further review, the memo said, warning that providers “must respond promptly to requests for information.”

In a statement, the Office of Refugee Resettlement said the change was driven by a review last year that found 95% of more than 9,000 reports “were determined not to be viable trafficking leads” for criminal investigators.

“The vast majority of the reports detailed instances of alleged abuse or neglect, not forced labor or commercial sex as defined in human trafficking statutes,” the statement said.

Even so, 58% of reports from shelter employees and case managers qualified for trafficking-related benefits. The change in reporting will “strengthen integrity, reduce improper referrals, reduce fraud, and ensure that children who may have experienced trafficking receive immediate support,” the statement said.

Former official questions rationale

Jen Smyers, who served as deputy director of the Office of Refugee Resettlement during the Biden administration, said the claim that the change will streamline reporting is questionable. She said ORR already gets the human trafficking reports but has no special expertise in evaluating them, unlike the office created for that purpose.

The fear is that legitimate claims will get delayed or missed during the new layer of review, and career employees will face political pressure to refer fewer cases, she said.

“It’s the opposite of streamlining,” Smyers said.

Smyers noted the change comes after what she called an “ onslaught ” of Trump administration policies that have undermined the ability of unaccompanied minors to gain legal status, including making it harder to leave federal custody, arresting sponsors in the middle of the release process, and cutting their legal representation.

“What they are trying to do is deport as many as possible. What interferes with deporting children is if they are eligible for protections Congress has given them,” she said.

text:
A federal judge has ruled that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) "likely violated" a U.S. citizen's First Amendment rights when immigration officials delivered a warning notice after he sent a critical email to the head of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), granting preliminary relief while the lawsuit moves forward.

In a 43-page opinion issued Tuesday, Judge Rudolph Contreras of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia found that plaintiff David Streever was likely to succeed on his claim that ICE officials improperly threatened him over constitutionally protected political speech. The judge concluded that a warning notice delivered to Streever's home could reasonably be interpreted as demanding that he stop criticizing ICE leadership and warning him of potential prosecution if he continued.

"Mr. Streever has a right to express his political views through non-threatening speech, however degrading the speech might be," Contreras wrote. The judge said the notice likely infringed on that right by threatening consequences if he did not stop criticizing government officials.

Read More on News

DHS argued that the warning was simply a reminder not to violate federal law and that the investigation into the email had already been closed. The government also maintained that ICE has a legitimate interest in investigating potential threats against officials, citing a significant increase in threats directed at agency personnel.

A DHS spokesperson told Newsweek that “any allegation DHS and its components are attempting to ‘squash’ free speech is categorically FALSE,” adding that ICE investigates all credible threats toward its employees, including threats to the ICE director.

The spokesperson said ICE officers “are on the frontlines arresting terrorists, gang members, murderers, child sex abusers, and rapists,” and are facing “coordinated campaigns of violence” that have resulted in a 1,300 percent increase in assaults, a 3,300 percent increase in vehicular attacks, and an 8,000 percent increase in death threats. “Anyone who assaults or threatens our law enforcement officers will face the consequences,” the spokesperson said.

Adam B. Steinbaugh, senior attorney at the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, told Newsweek, "The government has created a systematic means to intimidate critics into silence. Telling someone their political speech may land them in handcuffs violates the First Amendment just as arresting them would. That finding will help not only Mr. Streever, but establishes precedent other people can rely on when officials, state or federal, try to intimidate them into silence."

What Did Streever Say?

The ruling stems from a lawsuit filed by Streever, a U.S. citizen from New York, who challenged ICE's response to an email he sent on January 26 to then-Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons. In the email, Streever condemned Lyons over ICE's handling of the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minnesota, calling him a "monstrous human being" and comparing him to a Nazi. The court previously found the email contained no threat of physical violence.

"You are a monstrous human being and will go down in history as America's Reinhard Heydrich, the butcher," the email read.

"The way you are protecting the obvious execution in Minnesota, even as we see the videos, will lead to your downfall. Even Trump will turn on you before the end, and you will be a sad, despised man who eats himself alive with shame at your own pathetic weakness.

"You will never know peace. You will seek to lose yourself, to escape the burden of knowing the truth about yourself. But wherever you go, you will find yourself. You will torment yourself until your last day on Earth."

According to court records, ICE's Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) opened an investigation after determining that the email contained what officials described as "potential threatening undertones." OPR investigates allegations of misconduct involving ICE personnel.

“I’m deeply relieved that the court affirmed what I knew all along: that I am permitted to speak my conscience in the United States of America, including when I criticize government officials,” Streever said in a press release. “While I wish this ordeal hadn’t happened, hopefully this incident will serve as a reminder that the First Amendment protects us all.”

Immigration enforcement remains a flashpoint in national politics. Supporters of the Trump administration's deportation agenda have argued that aggressive enforcement is necessary to uphold immigration laws and protect public safety, while critics have raised concerns about the impact of some enforcement actions on civil liberties. The United States ranked 64th out of 180 countries in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index, its lowest position ever, according to Reporters Without Borders.

What Did ICE Do?

According to court filings, two ICE agents went to Streever's home in Rochester, New York, on June 23 and left a document labeled "WARNING NOTICE" with his wife, the Reverend Hilary Streever.

The notice said ICE's Office of Professional Responsibility had identified an email sent to Lyons that it believed might violate federal law and warned of potential prosecution.

The filings also say that agents later attempted to contact Streever while he and his 7-year-old daughter were returning from a trip to Europe. According to the court record, agents went to a hotel in New York City where Streever was staying after returning to the United States.

Court documents say a hotel employee informed Streever that a federal agent was trying to reach him. The filings further state that Streever subsequently received voicemail messages from individuals identifying themselves as federal agents seeking to speak with him about the investigation.

Court Rules 'Likely' Violation

In July, Streever sought emergency court intervention, arguing that ICE's response to the email had chilled his willingness to speak out against the agency. At the time, his attorneys argued that federal agents had tracked him down months after he sent the message and delivered a formal warning suggesting his criticism could violate federal law.

Contreras agreed that law enforcement agencies may investigate potential threats and declined to bar DHS from conducting future investigations. However, he found that the warning notice went beyond a routine inquiry and could reasonably be viewed as a threat of adverse government action directed at protected speech.

The judge wrote that the notice asked Streever to "discontinue" the behavior referenced in the investigation while warning him of possible prosecution and stating that receipt of the notice would be considered if he continued similar conduct. Taken together, the court found, the language could chill a reasonable person's willingness to engage in political expression.

"The Warning Notice demands that Mr. Streever discontinue his political speech and threatens consequences if he continues," the judge wrote.

The court also pointed to a statement on X issued by the official DHS account after the lawsuit was filed. In response to publicity surrounding the case, the account said that ICE investigates all credible threats against employees and said that anyone who threatens law enforcement officers would "face the consequences." Contreras said the statement reinforced Streever's argument that he faced an ongoing threat of government action.

As part of the preliminary injunction, the court ordered that DHS and ICE may not rely on the warning notice, may not use Streever's January 2026 email as a basis for future prosecutions or investigative demands during the litigation, and may not issue similar warnings suggesting that non-threatening criticism of the government is unlawful.

At the same time, Contreras rejected a request from attorneys that would have barred future investigations involving Streever altogether. The ruling emphasizes that the government retains authority to investigate potential threats and protect public officials, provided those investigations do not infringe protected speech.

The judge stayed the injunction for 14 days to allow the government an opportunity to appeal.

text:
INDIANAPOLIS — A five-day U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operation resulted in 426 arrests across Indiana, authorities say.

“Operation Safe Community-Indiana” ran from Aug.30 through Sept.3.

ICE says those arrested had criminal histories including sex crimes, assault, domestic violence, drug trafficking, weapons offenses, burglary, identity theft, and fraud. Authorities say members of gangs including MS-13, 18th Street, and Tren de Aragua were also among those arrested.

While much of the operation focused on the Indianapolis metro area, ICE officers conducted enforcement actions throughout the entire state.

“Every alien arrested during this operation was in violation of U.S. immigration law, and Indiana is safer today as a result of the hard work of our ICE officers,” ICE Chicago Deputy Field Office Director Raymond Hernandez said in a statement.

The department added the operation “is in keeping with President Trump’s promise to make America safe again.”

As News 8 previously reported, ICE’s presence had many residents in the community on edge.

In a shopping plaza in Lawrence, several businesses closed their doors, including a Haitian market and Honduran restaurant.

Lawrence Police Department said it helped ICE agents arrest a person with felony warrants at a hair salon on Pendleton Pike.

Lawrence police said they only became involved because the situation became a public safety issue, stressing that they did not plan or initiate the operation.

One woman told News 8 her brother was detained by ICE while at work.

Sightings of ICE across the city flooded social media.

U.S. Rep. Andre Carson sent a formal inquiry to ICE, demanding more details on the raids. He expressed his concern that some arrests were based on racial profiling.

“ICE claims they’re going after the worst of the worst,” he said. “That’s simply not true. Ninety-six percent of ICE arrests in July did not have prior criminal convictions. ICE is making our city less safe.”

Mayor Joe Hogsett also weighed in, saying the city received no advance notice from ICE about any operations in Marion County.

Operation Safe Community-Indiana follows similar enforcement actions in Atlanta and Washington, D.C. Indiana falls under ICE Chicago’s jurisdiction.

[00:00:03] George Whipple: Welcome to Employment Law This Week. I’m George Whipple. The current administration is stepping up enforcement on work-related visas. The Department of Labor has frozen all new PERM applications from several major IT and tech companies. PERM is a process by which a company proves that no qualified, willing, able, and available U.S. workers exist for a job.

[00:00:33] George Whipple: It’s the mandatory first step for most employment-based green card applications. This freeze is the most aggressive enforcement action to come out of a joint investigation by the DOL’s Office of Inspector General and the White House Fraud Task Force. Investigators are probing allegations of wage suppression, fake recruitment processes, and the systemic misuse of H-1B and PERM.

[00:01:03] George Whipple: This comes as the Department of Homeland Security is attempting for the second time to raise the fee for H-1B visas to six figures. The agency published a proposed rule to require an additional filing fee of $103,265 for any H-1B petition filed with the immigration agency. Meanwhile, the State Department has announced a pause on all immigrant visa applications coming from outside the U.S., and has begun preparations to revoke up to 200,000 business and tourism visas inside the country.

[00:01:44] George Whipple: The revocations would apply to visa holders who have sought asylum in the U.S. All of these actions are creating a climate of ambiguity that makes it more difficult for companies to attract foreign workers and ensure compliance while navigating the visa process. Agricultural employers are contending with a different kind of ambiguity after a California federal judge ruled that the Department of Labor’s rules for calculating the Adverse Effect Wage Rate for H-2A farmworkers are unlawful.

[00:02:19] George Whipple: The decision kept the rates in place, but directed the department to develop a new methodology for calculating the rates. The DOL is also required to notify employers that they may be held responsible for back pay covering the difference between the rates. Agricultural employers are already facing immigration headwinds, with ICE enforcement resulting in a sustained increase in raids at their facilities.

INDIANAPOLIS, Ind. (WGN) — More than 400 people were taken into custody during an immigration enforcement operation in Indiana that began late last month.

According to officials from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the five-day operation, titled, “Operation Safe Community-Indiana,” which unfolded between Aug. 30 and Sept. 3, resulted in the arrest of 426 individuals described as “illegal alien offenders.”

ICE officials said the arrests involved individuals with criminal histories that include sex crimes, assault and battery, domestic assault, drug trafficking, assault with a dangerous weapon, other weapons crimes, fraud, identity theft, burglary, property damage, driving while intoxicated, public order crimes and more.

“Operation Safe Community-Indiana reflects ICE’s continued commitment to protecting Hoosier communities by working alongside our state and local law enforcement partners to arrest and remove criminal alien offenders who pose threats to public safety,” ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations acting Assistant Director Patricia Hyde said in a press release shared Wednesday. “Over the course of this five-day operation, ICE officers, in coordination with state and local law enforcement partners, arrested 426 illegal alien offenders across Indiana, including individuals with criminal histories involving sex crimes, assault, domestic violence, drug trafficking, weapons offenses and more. This operation underscores the fact that when law enforcement agencies cooperate, the American people are safer. We thank our state and local partners for their support and continued commitment to protecting communities across Indiana and the nation.”

text:
Dozens of detainees at Florida's now-shuttered immigrant detention center "Alligator Alcatraz" were held in 18-square-foot outdoor cages — about the same size as telephone booths — according to a new report by the Department of Homeland Security's Office of Inspector General.

The report, dated Sept. 11 but published Sept. 14, detailed a January 2026 inspection of the facility, which was officially named the Florida Soft-Sided Facility. "Alligator Alcatraz" was shuttered in June.

The report detailed unhygienic conditions in the facility, such as bug-infested showers, and only allowing detainees to shower three times per week, instead of daily, as standards require. It also found food stored at improper temperatures and dirty drinking water.

David Spicer, director of policy and engagement for migration at the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, told OSV News, "These findings from the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's [DHS] independent oversight agency are quite disturbing."

"Unfortunately, such violations of the government's own detention standards are also not entirely surprising," he said. "Whether it's ensuring equal access to religious services or abiding by protections specific to families and children, the government's detention standards are only credible if they're consistently upheld across all detention facilities.

"This is among the reasons why the USCCB has repeatedly urged regular oversight by both the federal agencies charged with that responsibility and Congress."

"The immense pressure currently being exerted on DHS to expand immigration detention capacity as quickly as possible — using the influx of funding received by the Department over the past year — merely exacerbates the need for this oversight," Spicer added.

As Bishop Brendan J. Cahill of Victoria, chairman of the U.S. bishops' Committee on Migration, "said earlier this year," he noted, "these issues should be a cause for deeper reflection. Ultimately, this is about protecting human life and dignity, and the immigration status of those in these detention facilities make them no less deserving of that protection."

Among the report's findings were that the Florida facility "confined 79 detainees in small metal enclosures — each offering about 18 square feet of floor space — for periods ranging from several minutes to nearly 2 hours, a practice unlike any OIG team has observed in ICE facilities."

"The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment," the report said.

The report said staff at the facility described the small metal enclosures — which measured approximately 4 feet 3 inches wide on each side and 7 feet 9 inches tall — as "calming areas" for detainees "to deescalate and have time alone."

Alex Lanfranconi, communications director for Gov. Ron DeSantis, R-Fla., argued in a statement that "left-wing media wants to focus on a confinement area for violent criminal aliens who have proven they cannot remain peaceful while awaiting deportation."

"While it adheres to all federal standards for criminal confinement, we'd make it even smaller if we could," Lanfranconi added.

Anna Gallagher, executive director of the Catholic Legal Immigration Network, also known as CLINIC, told OSV News, "The findings in this report are horrifying."

"Confining people in tiny metal enclosures for hours is inhumane, and it should never be normalized as part of our immigration system," she said. "Our Catholic faith calls us to recognize the God-given dignity of every person, and these practices violate that fundamental commitment. This report demands accountability and immediate action to ensure every person in government custody is treated with the dignity they deserve."

The report said staff at the facility "could not clearly identify which detention standards they used," and that the absence of "well-defined standards at detention facilities increases the risk that detainees may not receive appropriate care."

The inspector general therefore compared conditions at the facility against both Florida Model Jail Standards and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's National Detention Standards 2019 and "applied the more restrictive standard to support our findings."

Kevin Appleby, senior fellow for policy and communications at the Center for Migration Studies of New York and the former director of migration policy for the USCCB, told OSV News, "I think this report might be the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the inhumane treatment of detainees in immigration detention."

"In the One Big Beautiful Bill, Congress basically wrote a blank check for ICE to expand detention facilities without any oversight, so we will sadly see more of this type of treatment around the country," Appleby said.

He added, "Credit is due" to Archbishop Thomas G. Wenski and the Archdiocese of Miami "for putting pressure on DHS to close Alligator Alcatraz."

"Similar campaigns should be launched in other dioceses in which new detention facilities are being built," he said.

Wenski's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In its response to the inspector general report, the Department of Homeland Security said it would not be implementing the recommendations for improving the facility since "the FSSF has been permanently closed."
