text:
KNOXVILLE, Tenn. (WATE) — The Knox County Sheriff’s Office has signed an agreement to expand its involvement in federal immigration enforcement.

The sheriff’s office has participated in the 287(g) program since 2017 under the “Jail Enforcement Model,” meaning some officers can investigate people in jail who have active or pending criminal charges for potential immigration violations.

According to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement website, KCSO signed a memorandum of agreement on Friday, Sept. 11 to implement the 287(g) program’s “Task Force Model.” Under this model, qualified deputies are granted immigration powers that can be enforced while conducting routine police duties or while participating in an ICE-led task force.

New Knox County Sheriff Brent Gibson expressed support for working more closely with ICE during his campaign and said he would move to the Task Force Model in a recent interview on Tennessee This Week.

The sheriff’s office would nominate officers to participate under the Task Force Model. Nominees must have at least two years of law enforcement experience, be a U.S. citizen, and complete and pass a background investigation.

text:
Officials are investigating reports that the warehouse is being used to hold immigrants. Federal authorities say they have not decided how they will use the site.

New Jersey officials are investigating reports that federal immigration authorities have used a Roxbury warehouse to hold immigrants and will ask a federal judge to intervene if they determine the activity violated a court order restricting use of the property.

The disclosure came in a joint status report filed Sept. 15 in U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey, where New Jersey and Roxbury Township officials sued the federal government in March over plans to turn a warehouse on Route 46 into an immigration detention center.

Attorneys for New Jersey, Roxbury and the federal government filed the status report Tuesday to update U.S. District Judge Jamel Semper on the case. Attorneys for New Jersey and Roxbury said in the report that officials recently learned of reports that the warehouse had been used in connection with immigration enforcement and were investigating whether that activity violated an earlier court order.

“If they determine that Defendants have not complied with the stipulated order, Plaintiffs will seek appropriate relief from the Court,” state lawyers wrote in the filing.

The status report also says federal officials have not decided whether to turn the warehouse into an immigration detention center, despite telling the court in June that they had abandoned the project and planned to sell the property.

“Defendants continue to assess whether to proceed with plans to convert the Roxbury Warehouse into a detention facility,” lawyers for the Trump administration wrote in the Sept. 15 report. “At present, there is no timeline for reaching that decision.”

That position is different from what attorneys for the parties told the same federal court on June 29.

“Defendants no longer intend to convert the Roxbury Warehouse into an immigration detention facility and intend to sell the warehouse,” they wrote in a June filing.

But federal officials later reconsidered. Justice Department attorneys notified the court July 10 that the Department of Homeland Security was again weighing whether to convert the warehouse into a detention center. A July 17 status report said federal officials were still assessing whether to proceed and had no timeline for making a decision.

Two months later, federal officials still have not decided what to do with the warehouse.

The latest filing comes after activists raised concerns that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials were already using the warehouse as a temporary holding and transfer site for immigrants arrested nearby.

Project NINJA, short for No ICE North Jersey Alliance, asked New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport on Monday to investigate what the group said was evidence that ICE officials had used the warehouse to hold immigrants temporarily.

The group pointed to the experience of a man arrested by ICE officials during an enforcement operation in Dover on Sept. 4. The man told his family he had been taken to a “jail or prison” before being transferred to an immigration detention center in Elizabeth, according to Project NINJA.

Activists collected videos of federal agents detaining immigrants in the Dover area and of vehicles with the same license plates later entering and leaving the warehouse.

As part of a May agreement, federal officials agreed not to take steps to convert the Roxbury warehouse into a detention center, other than certain security and maintenance work, until they complete an environmental assessment.

Federal officials can install temporary fencing, security cameras, lighting and signs; change locks; maintain heating, cooling and electrical systems; test plumbing; maintain fire protection systems; clean the building and remove garbage; maintain the grounds; and perform other limited work needed to keep the property secure.

The agreement restricts activities intended to convert the property into a detention center, except for the specified security and maintenance work.

On Tuesday, the Department of Homeland Security did not answer The Vindicator’s question about whether the warehouse is being used to hold immigrants, instead citing the pending lawsuit.

“Due to ongoing litigation, DHS has no further comment at this time,” a spokesperson wrote.

Semper has ordered lawyers for both sides to file their next status report by Nov. 16.

text:
Northern Virginia congressional candidates are facing off on the future of immigration enforcement, a proposed triumphal arch and the role of AI and data centers.

The issues all took center stage in a Sept. 8 candidate forum sponsored by the Arlington County Civic Federation, where Rep. Don Beyer (D-8) faced three challengers.

Beyer gave the most blunt response to a question about the future of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“We need to shut down ICE,” he said.

The agency’s culture is “irretrievably destroyed,” Beyer added.

His challengers offered differing takes on the agency and its management. Republican Tony Sabio attempted a middle-ground approach.

“We have to have accountability … but we cannot throw a whole system out,” he said.

“I don’t think that I’d defund ICE,” said Shelly Arnoldi, the Libertarian candidate.

Arnoldi said she would like to see many of those without legal status depart the U.S.

“Anyone that’s here illegally should return [to their home], especially those who are taking free stuff,” she said.

Tim Sharman, an independent, said, “ICE needs to be reconstituted.”

Each candidate had only a minute to answer the question, which was paired with a second one: How did candidates feel about President Donald Trump’s planned memorial arch near Arlington National Cemetery?

Beyer called the arch “stupid.” Sharman called it “absurd” and “a giant waste of money.” Arnoldi said she would vote to “stop funding all the monuments,” along with the National Gallery of Art and the Smithsonian.

Republican Sabio didn’t answer the arch question head-on. He spoke more generally of government funding: “If it doesn’t return investment to the people, I will not support it,” he said.

Responding to a question focused on artificial intelligence and the data centers needed to power its growth, candidates also split.

All voiced concern, but several added there shouldn’t be rushed efforts to corral them at the expense of the good they can provide.

“I understand there’s a risk, there’s nefarious actors, [but] we should not be scared of technology,” Sabio said.

Beyer, too, said AI had the potential to be a net plus, pointing to healthcare advances already in the pipeline.

“There’s a lot of good that can come from it,” he said.

But with public opinion souring on the data centers required to power AI programming, candidates either added caveats to their support, or expressed the desire to pull back.

“Halt things right now, until we know what’s going on,” Arnoldi said of the proliferation of data centers across Northern Virginia and the nation.

As for artificial intelligence? “AI has been rolled out too quickly,” she said. “I don’t trust our government to control it.”

Sharman feared impacts on the nation’s workforce if AI causes mass displacement in significant industries.

On data centers, he said he did not want a one-size-fits-all policy handed down from the federal government.

“It needs to be a local decision,” Sharman said.

In the 40-minute debate, candidates also tackled the increasingly controversial use of Flock license-plate readers and whether Beyer’s experience should be enough to merit him a new two-year term.

The 8th District includes all of Arlington, portions of eastern Fairfax County, and the cities of Alexandria and Falls Church. Beyer, a former lieutenant governor, was elected in 2014, succeeding Jim Moran, and fended off four challengers in the Aug. 4 Democratic primary.

The inner suburbs of Northern Virginia are Democratic bastions, but Civic Federation president Nicholas Giacobbe said political forums were an opportunity for the public to hear from all candidates seeking their vote.

“There are a lot of different opinions, lots of different positions,” he said of the field of contenders gathered on Sept. 8.

name: Human Rights
title: The government might strip some asylum seekers of their work rights. Here's why it shouldn't
description:
Withdrawing asylum seekers’ work rights would not stop them from working.
Work rights on these visas depend on the specific bridging visa that asylum seekers are granted.
The experiences of asylum seekers in countries without work rights, such as the United Kingdom, confirm this.
Asylum seekers without work rights engaged in unauthorised work and were easily exploited by employers.
Even when asylum applications are unsuccessful, the voluntary return or deportation of asylum seekers can be delayed or not feasible.
text:
Migration is never far from the headlines, but it’s particularly topical this week in the wake of One Nation announcing its policy on the subject.

It comes as the federal government is expected to announce its policy on the topic in coming days. While no firm details have been revealed, it’s been reported the government is considering restricting the work rights of asylum seekers while they appeal visa rejections.

Should the government decide to do that, there is little doubt it would have dire consequences for the livelihood and wellbeing of asylum seekers.

We know this because our research shows early access to work rights and other government support significantly improves employment outcomes for asylum seekers in Australia. The benefits of early work rights continue to matter even after ten years of permanent residency in Australia.

Withdrawing asylum seekers’ work rights would not stop them from working. Instead, it would push them into precarious, unsafe and exploitative employment. In turn, this would create an even more vulnerable population requiring further support down the track.

Who gets to work?

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, to which Australia is a signatory, guarantees all people the right to work.

For asylum seekers in Australia, that’s only partially true. Some are allowed to work in Australia, but work eligibility depends on the specific type of visa granted.

The most consequential are bridging visas, which are temporary visas that allow asylum seekers to legally reside in Australia while their asylum applications are under review or while they appeal a visa decision, or make plans to leave Australia.

Work rights on these visas depend on the specific bridging visa that asylum seekers are granted. Some people receive bridging visas with a condition that prohibits work rights.

Asylum seekers granted temporary protection visas and safe haven protection visas have the right to work.

The benefits of work

Paid employment has material, social, personal and psychosocial benefits for asylum seekers.

Employment provides a way for asylum seekers to support themselves financially. But it also promotes individual health and wellbeing benefits, such as self-realisation and dignity.

Previous research shows paid employment is a source of empowerment, increasing self-worth and hope for the future.

Employment also supports integration into Australian society. A workplace is a site of social connection that can foster relationships beyond the immediate family and ethnic networks.

Our research published in the Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies shows asylum seekers with immediate work rights in Australia have better short-term and long-term labour market outcomes.

They also report feeling a sense of security. In addition to enhancing financial security, work rights offer stability and reassurance during a highly vulnerable period marked by uncertainty about one’s immigration status and restricted access to government support.

What happens if they can’t work?

Research also shows that prohibiting work rights among temporary migrants does not discourage them from working, but rather pushes them further into precarious and exploitative employment.

The experiences of asylum seekers in countries without work rights, such as the United Kingdom, confirm this. Asylum seekers without work rights engaged in unauthorised work and were easily exploited by employers.

They were often paid late and below the minimum wage. Some circumvented their work restrictions by acquiring false paperwork and were subject to criminal convictions after being caught.

Asylum cases are complex. Even when asylum applications are unsuccessful, the voluntary return or deportation of asylum seekers can be delayed or not feasible. This can happen if foreign governments do not cooperate or provide travel documents to return asylum seekers.

Under these circumstances, asylum seekers still need a financial way to support themselves until they leave the country.

Asylum seekers can also appeal visa rejections, which may well be successful. With little access to government support, they need to be able to finance their lives while these processes play out.

The denial of work rights may also create other unintended consequences for the government, including dependence on state welfare for those eligible, or community sector support.

Highly visible targets

Debates about immigration are at fever pitch with a focus on reducing the numbers of migrants coming to Australia.

Asylum seekers are a particularly visible type of migrant. They’ve long been subject to negative public perceptions and widespread misunderstanding, largely as a result of intense political campaigns.

In response, successive Australian governments have adopted increasingly restrictive measures, including mandatory detention as a means of managing asylum seekers and deterring further migration.

In this way, any attempt to curtail the rights of asylum seekers would fit into a decades-long bipartisan pattern of targeting a very small group of migrants.

Read more: Australia has spent 25 years ‘stopping the boats’, but that’s not the same as controlling migration

What should be done instead?

Evidence-based policy suggests providing early access to rights, including work rights, is crucial.

The timing is key. Integration is a long process. Immediate access to employment, housing and training can help people feel at home in, and contribute to, their new home country sooner.

This is a key takeaway from Sweden and Norway, where humanitarian immigrants had early access to work rights and other government support.

title: Deportation decision for Salah Sarsour expected before end of September
description:
Jawad Boulos, who represented Sarsour as an attorney in the West Bank, addressed the military court record from the 1990s.
The lenient deal was evidence to Boulos that even the Israelis did not take their own accusations against Sarsour seriously.
He added that Sarsour never mentioned having gone to the hospital due to torture, and that Israeli court records don’t mention that he claimed he was abused by the Israeli interrogators.

text:
The fate of Salah Sarsour, president of the Islamic Society of Milwaukee, is now in the hands of a federal immigration judge in Kansas City who, by Sept. 30, will decide whether Sarsour can be deported from the place where he has lived as a legal permanent resident for over 30 years.

Monday concluded court testimony from experts and witnesses in Sarsour’s deportation case. Sarsour was arrested in late March by armed federal immigration agents in Milwaukee. He had never been arrested in the United States before.

“What’s at stake here is not just whether this good man can stay here, but whether people can speak freely in this country without fear of unlawful retribution,” Sarsour’s lawyer Patrick Taurel said after the Monday hearing.

The Department of Homeland Security claimed that Sarsour lied on his green card application when he came to the United States in the late 1990s. DHS also claims that Sarsour, a Palestinian man, had been convicted in Israeli military courts of throwing Molotov cocktails at the homes of Israeli soldiers in 1988, and separately accused of illegally attempting to possess weapons and ammunition in 1995.

Taurel, representing Sarsour, disputed those accusations Monday saying DHS had broadcast them in “libelous press releases.” Taurel said Sarsour had been detained as a Palestinian teenager by Israel’s occupying army and convicted in military court for throwing stones and disorderly conduct, not for throwing Molotov cocktails. This occurred during the First Intifada, a mass Palestinian uprising against the Israeli army which lasted from 1987 to 1993.

Amahl Bishara, a professor at Tufts University, testified during one of Sarsour’s hearings in late July that stone throwing was an act of political expression against the occupation carried out by Palestinian youth. Taruel described it as “a kind of screaming into the void that they don’t approve of the occupation,” during a Monday press conference.

Jawad Boulos, who represented Sarsour as an attorney in the West Bank, addressed the military court record from the 1990s.

He recommended that Sarsour take a plea in the 1995 case because the Israelis were offering what Boulos felt was an unusually good deal by reducing four charges to just one of procuring weapons, and having Sarsour agree to time served. The plea deal also allowed Sarsour to avoid waiting up to two more years in detention for a trial. The lenient deal was evidence to Boulos that even the Israelis did not take their own accusations against Sarsour seriously.

Responding to DHS arguments that if Sarsour were tortured the record of his imprisonment would have shown that he suffered harm, Boulos said that the Israeli authorities sometimes did not allow him to see his client. He noted a no-contact order among the Israeli documents barring Boulos from seeing Sarsour during the first several weeks of Sarsour’s confinement. During hearings in July, Sari Bashi, an Israeli lawyer and human rights investigator, described the West Bank, where Sarsour grew up, as a place under “belligerent occupation” where confessions are coerced through torture, and the local Israeli commander acts as the executive, lawmaker, judge, and executor of law.

Dr. Jackie Bashkoff, a forensic psychologist, testified in July that after evaluating Sarsour, she determined that he suffers from Post Traumatic Stress Disorder stemming from his experiences of being tortured.

Prosecutors said Monday that Sarsour’s defense team “completely glossed over” that Sarsour never “complained about mistreatment” by the Israelis. “That silence says everything,” said attorney Scott Jebson, representing the Department of Homeland Security. He added that Sarsour never mentioned having gone to the hospital due to torture, and that Israeli court records don’t mention that he claimed he was abused by the Israeli interrogators.

In earlier hearings, prosecutors also attempted to cast doubt on Sarsour’s PTSD diagnosis. Jebson said that Dr. Bashkoff used “buzz words” to describe Sarsour as having a “startle response.” Prosecutors also suggested in earlier hearings that symptoms of his type 2 diabetes could be confused for PTSD. “I can go through every witness they called” and discredit or undermine their testimony, Jebson told the judge on Monday.

Besides Sarsour’s detention by Israeli authorities, DHS is also accusing him of attempting to register to vote despite not being a U.S. citizen in the lead-up to the 2004 elections. Prosecutors have pointed to a voter registration card with Sarsour’s name on it.

Sarsour never attempted to cast a ballot, and his defense team suggested that the registration card could be linked to documented problems with a voter registration drive involving about 3,000 special registration deputies in Milwaukee. The Legislative Audit Bureau issued a letter in 2005 highlighting problems with the deputies. “Some special registration deputies are municipal officials, but many work for interest groups or political parties,” the report read. “Problems have been identified with registrations completed by some special registration deputies, including inaccurate, illegible, and falsified registration forms.”

Taurel said Sarsour had no recollection of signing the card and that when he learned about it in 2009, he took steps to remove it. Taurel also said that even if Sarsour signed the card it wouldn’t matter because he never actually voted, and thus would not have received a benefit by claiming to be a U.S. citizen under the law.

Mark Robel, an FBI polygraph examiner, testified in July that he examined Sarsour asking him whether he ever knowingly voted as a non-citizen during the 2004 election and whether he ever registered to vote. Robel said Sarsour passed the polygraph with no deception detected. “If he had tried to register to vote in any election, he would not have passed that test,” Robel told prosecutors when they questioned the polygraph’s accuracy.

A check of MyVote Wisconsin shows that Sarsour is not currently registered to vote.

Taurel said the Trump administration has targeted Sarsour because of his outspoken advocacy for Palestinian rights. “We are here because of Salah’s speech,” he said. “I’m not speculating about this,” Taurel said, citing the government’s reasoning in the case, which claims Sarsour is a national security threat. “The reason they arrested him, the reason we’re here, is his speech.”

In June, Sarsour was released from an Indiana immigration detention center, where he was held for more than 80 days. He was ordered released by a Trump-appointed federal judge, who ruled that Sarsour had a “substantial” claim that his arrest was First Amendment retaliation.

Sarsour is both the president of Wisconsin’s largest mosque and a board member of American Muslims for Palestine, which has been labeled by the conservative Heritage Foundation as part of a support network for Hamas.

In June 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued a memorandum stating that Sarsour was eligible for deportation because “his actions undermine U.S. foreign policy.” In February of this year, the Justice Department announced that it would target groups like American Muslims for Palestine. The following month in March, Sarsour’s profile on a pro-Israel doxxing website called the Canary Mission was updated. Four days later he was arrested by federal immigration agents.

Taurel said that while he believes that Sarsour has a strong case against being deported, immigration judges are under extraordinary pressure from the Trump administration and the neutrality of the immigration court system “has been severely undermined.”

The judge in Sarsour’s immigration case, Jayme Salinardi, is expected to make a ruling on whether he can be deported by the end of the month. The Milwaukee Journal Sentinel reports that Salinardi has a record of denying asylum claims 90% of the time — far above the national average of 59%. A Democratic appointee, he previously worked as an attorney for ICE.

On Sept. 30, the court will hold a status conference on the case. If the judge decides that Sarsour can be deported, then his attorneys will push for relief. Taurel said that “we fear the worst,” if he is sent back to Israel-occupied territory.

Taurel said that Sarsour is not backing down, adding that Sarsour will appear with Taruel on a podcast in the coming weeks, and is expected to travel to Washington D.C. to speak with elected officials. “Salah refuses to be cowed by this,” he said on Monday. “He is a brave, courageous advocate for Palestine. He won’t be silenced. He is not required to be muzzled in any way.”

description:

text:
More than 300 South Korean workers who were swept up in last year’s immigration raid at a Hyundai electric-vehicle manufacturing plant in Georgia are challenging the US government, in the first major legal action over one of the largest immigration enforcement operations under President Donald Trump.

Administrative claims on behalf of the workers, a mandatory step before a federal lawsuit, have begun to be filed with nine federal agencies, including the Department of Homeland Security, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Customs and Border Protection, the FBI and the Departments of Justice and Labor, a lawyer representing the claimants told CNN.

Documentation supporting that the first individual claim had been mailed to the agencies was shared with CNN by the lawyer, a Korean attorney practicing in Georgia who has been representing those workers. She asked to be identified only as a Korean lawyer practicing in Georgia, saying it matters to her that the detainees are represented by one of their own. The lawyer said she aims to have all claims filed by end of the year.

The September 4 raid in Ellabell, Georgia, around 25 miles west of Savannah, was the largest single-site operation in the history of Homeland Security Investigations, authorities said at the time. Nearly 500 federal, state and local officers descended on the sprawling plant, detaining 475 workers, mostly South Koreans. Many ranged in age from 20s to 60s, said Kim, one of the lead organizers, whom CNN is identifying only by his surname.

Several workers CNN spoke to allege they were unlawfully arrested and detained without explanation or interpreters, shackled, forced to sign documents they couldn’t understand and held in overcrowded cells. Despite the treatment, some have since returned to the US, saying it’s a necessary part of their job.

According to a search warrant obtained by CNN, the federal immigration operation in Ellabell named just four target individuals – none of them the Korean workers.

Kim provided CNN with his claim, the first to be filed, which argues that he was unlawfully detained and “subjected to demeaning living conditions” while in an ICE facility for seven days, adding the raid resulted in “intentional infliction of emotional distress, humiliation… and lasting psychological trauma.”

The claim seeks damages for confiscated belongings, lost work and psychological harm, and alleges false imprisonment, abuse of process and intentional infliction of emotional distress. The lawyer told CNN each of the 300 workers had similar claims and declined to specify the amount of damages sought.

The aim of filing claims, the attorney said, is to make the US government acknowledge an “enormous, unjust mistake” and “admit it and apologize.”

“The US government used the false pretext of finding four undocumented people to send hundreds of agents in full armor to storm the worksite of a Korean company that is one of the largest contributors to the American economy,” the attorney told CNN. “Before the whole world, they put engineers who had come lawfully to install equipment in handcuffs and shackles and paraded them like criminals, shaming all Koreans before the world as if Korean companies were invading the US labor market.”

CNN reached out to all nine agencies, but only received responses from DHS and CBP.

In a response to CNN’s inquiry, DHS said ICE “executed a judicial search warrant as part of an ongoing criminal investigation into allegations of unlawful employment practices and other serious federal crimes.” CBP referred CNN to a September 2025 release, which said those arrested “were found to be working illegally, in violation of the terms of their visas and/or statuses.”

All those taken into custody were suspected of living and working illegally in the US, said Steven Schrank, a Homeland Security Investigations special agent in charge, at the time of the detentions. Some had entered illegally, some had overstayed visas, and some had visa waivers that prohibited working, he said.

Four workers among those detained, who asked not to be fully identified for fear of retaliation, told CNN they were working under valid visas and were given no reason for their arrest when they were taken into custody.

“Even after being fully detained, we didn’t know why we were taken, or what crime we’d committed. No one knew anything. Everyone was just bewildered,” said Ryu, a detained worker who CNN is identifying by a pseudonym.

“There was no proper explanation, and yet this happened to us,” Kim said. “If they had at least explained things while proceeding, I might have understood a little.”

When asked whether the workers’ activities violated the terms of their visas, and why some have since re-entered on the same visas to do the same work, CBP told CNN that admissibility decisions are “made on a case-by-case basis” and that “having a non-immigrant visa from a US Embassy or Consulate, or an approved ESTA does not guarantee that you will be admitted into the United States.”

Asked about the raid, DHS pointed CNN to the White House, which later referred CNN to Trump’s Truth Social post last year urging foreign companies to “bring their people of expertise for a period of time to teach and train our people,” then “phase out” and go home.

Taken into ICE detention

The raid has largely been seen as a collision of two Trump priorities: bolstering American manufacturing while enforcing a hardline immigration campaign that has seen mass deportations drain the country’s labor force across manufacturing, agriculture and services.

The 2,900-acre Hyundai Metaplant has two parts: a Hyundai electric-vehicle manufacturing site and an EV battery plant then under construction, a joint venture with LG, where many of the detained Koreans were working.

Kim told CNN he and other workers were held for hours with no Korean interpreters present. They were ordered to sign documents they couldn’t read and later learned were consent-to-arrest forms, workers told CNN. Several signed, believing their agreement would send them home faster.

Kim said they were cuffed at the wrists and ankles and loaded onto buses to a detention center in Folkston, Georgia, where they spent about a week. For the first few days, they were held in a room crammed with up to 80 men, with just a handful of open toilets, in frigid conditions and with only a thin towel to sleep under, before being moved to two-person cells. Some had nothing to sleep under, he said. The food smelled sour and the water tasted off, several said.

Their stories echo those of other detainees across the US alleging packed rooms, inedible food and limited medical care. Such conditions have sparked protests – including last month outside an ICE facility in New Jersey – and several federal lawsuits.

Officers later presented them with voluntary-departure agreements, again with little explanation and without a translator, Kim said. When Kim demanded to know what he had done wrong, an officer said being inside the factory was the violation, warning that contesting it could take months – and, according to his claim, he was told by one agent, “They might torture you.” He signed. So did all the Korean detainees except one, who was married to a US citizen.

ICE did not respond to CNN’s request for comment on the alleged threat against Kim.

Ryu said he was among the workers held longest in the facility, those who entered on visa waivers rather than as B-1 visa holders. He told CNN he returned home nearly 10 pounds lighter. Months later, he was back at the same Georgia plant, where he worked as a project manager.

Pursuing accountability

The claims filed under the Federal Tort Claims Act not only paves the way for a federal lawsuit, but can also force the government to provide financial payment and put on the record why the workers were detained, what evidence justified it, and whether officers followed or broke agency policy, said Nora Engstrom, a Stanford law professor and tort expert not involved in the case.

If DHS does not respond to their claims within six months, the workers can take the case to federal court, according to the FTCA. Because the FTCA borrows state law, the workers would have to prove unlawful arrest under Georgia law, she said.

The government, she said, will “almost certainly” argue that the claim is barred by protections for injuries caused by federal employees carrying out “discretionary” duties – though that exception was never meant “to create blanket immunity for federal officers.”

The tort claims act requires each person to exhaust their own remedies before the government – one filing cannot speak for all, said James E. Pfander, a Northwestern law professor who studies the federal courts and is also not part of the case.

In the past, workers bringing similar claims have settled for significant damages. After a 2018 raid at a Tennessee meatpacking plant, detained workers alleging racial profiling, excessive force and unlawful arrest – some under the FTCA – settled with the government for more than $1 million, the workers’ attorneys said.

The FTCA is “the only reliable avenue for money damages,” said Kate Goettel, a former senior legal director for the American Immigration Council. Plaintiffs can also sue individual officers for constitutional violations, but the Supreme Court has increasingly shut that door, especially in immigration cases, said Goettel, who is also not involved in the case.

Choi, a field engineer who has since returned to the same Georgia plant, said the claim is about vindication.

“The thing that angers me the most is that there hasn’t been any kind of apology,” he said. “We were all taken, locked up, and left the US as if we were expelled. The impression we got is: ‘We thought you came illegally, so we just arrested you, but since that’s not the case, we’ll let you go. Come back to work if you want, or don’t.’”

A reliance on foreign specialists

For years, Washington has pressed Seoul to invest on American soil, most recently wielding tariff threats to extract some $350 billion in commitments. The Hyundai-LG battery plant is one of South Korea’s big bets.

The raid initially shut down construction, with the battery plant’s operator, HL-GA Battery Co., telling the Associated Press in November that work had resumed with a mix of new and returning workers – including some of the South Korean nationals detained in September.

The facility is now complete and commercial production began in April, the joint venture HLBMA told CNN, with its first shipment of battery cells delivered in May. The company said it now has “more than 500 employees on site, the majority hired locally.”

For highly technical projects, it may “draw on specialized expertise from outside the country,” but “all workers must fully comply with US laws and regulations,” it added.

Industry officials say US manufacturers often rely on foreign specialists to build and launch such plants, but that the visa system does not easily accommodate the assignments those projects require.

Some of the workers CNN spoke to said they had previously used the same business visas to work at battery plants across the US without trouble, including the B-1 business visitor visa, which permits training and setup, but bars production work or receiving a US paycheck.

Kim said they followed those rules while working in Ellabell, were paid in South Korean currency and provided “a great deal of training” to American workers, a process that takes time.

“Our work is highly specialized. No matter how much you provide manuals or training, in certain areas they can’t reach the same level of proficiency that we have,” he said.

In a statement to CNN, LG Energy Solution said it “prioritize(s) strict compliance” and sends experts only temporarily until plants can run on their own.

ICE and South Korea’s Foreign Ministry did not respond to CNN’s questions about the legal basis for the raid, the detention conditions, or the workers’ return on the same visas.

Since the raid, many have returned to work at US battery plants doing similar jobs, often on the same visas, while carrying the fear of being swept up again by immigration agents, the workers told CNN.

Jung, a software engineer, flew to Cleveland in June for equipment work and stayed through August. It is the only trade he has ever known, and his only way to make a living. “Even though I’m still scared,” he said, “I have no choice but to go.”

Kim later installed and repaired lithium-ion battery equipment in Lansing, Michigan, on the same B-1 visa he held the morning agents stormed the Georgia plant. He has since returned to South Korea.

Workers returning to the US carry a company-issued card listing their visa, employer and job, “in case immigration enforcement comes again,” Kim said – a new procedure since the Georgia raid.

“Before, my image of the US was that it’s a powerful country, a wealthy country, an ally,” Kim said. “So I didn’t really feel anxious.” That image, he said, “has been greatly shattered.”

“It’s not really that fair, or the land of freedom that we generally think of.”

Families who lost loved ones in crimes involving undocumented immigrants testified before Congress on Tuesday as House lawmakers renewed a contentious debate over so-called sanctuary policies and cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

The House Judiciary Subcommittee on Immigration Integrity, Security, and Enforcement examined policies in California, Oregon and New York that limit some cooperation between state and local authorities and federal immigration enforcement. (TNND)

The House Judiciary Subcommittee on Immigration Integrity, Security, and Enforcement examined policies in California, Oregon and New York that limit some cooperation between state and local authorities and federal immigration enforcement.

Elizabeth Carter told lawmakers her son and daughter-in-law were killed just 16 days after their wedding when an undocumented immigrant driving a truck crashed into them.

“Sanctuary policies have ... divided my life into before and after,” Carter testified.

According to the House Judiciary Committee, the driver had been issued a commercial driver's license by California.

Anatoly Varfolomeev also testified about the death of his 19-year-old daughter, Anya, who was killed along with a friend by an undocumented immigrant driving drunk in California in 2021.

Republicans pointed to the families' cases as evidence that sanctuary policies can prevent federal immigration authorities from removing potentially dangerous people from communities.

Rep. Tom McClintock, R-Calif., chairman of the subcommittee, argued the policies have contributed to preventable crimes and called for greater cooperation with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Democrats disputed that assessment and argued the Trump administration's immigration crackdown can make communities less safe by diverting federal law enforcement resources from other priorities.

Naureen Shah, director of government affairs in the American Civil Liberties Union's Equality Division, testified as the Democratic witness and criticized aggressive ICE enforcement operations.

Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., pointed to the July death of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston. The 52-year-old father was fatally shot by an ICE officer during an immigration operation. The Department of Homeland Security later acknowledged that Salgado Araujo was not the operation's intended target, saying he “resembled the target.” DHS has said the officer fired after Salgado Araujo rammed an ICE vehicle. His family has disputed the government's account.

The congressional debate comes as Republicans push H.R. 7640, dubbed the “Shut Down Sanctuary Policies Act of 2026.”

The legislation would require greater state and local cooperation with federal immigration authorities and could withhold certain federal funding from jurisdictions that refuse to comply with ICE detainers.

The House Judiciary Committee approved an amended version of the legislation earlier this year and recommended its passage.

McClintock said Tuesday that House leaders have assured him the legislation will be taken up before the current Congress ends in January, potentially moving the long-running fight over sanctuary policies from the committee room to the House floor.

text:
On Sept. 14, 2026, in Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration v. DHS, a federal court postponed implementation of the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) final rule that would have replaced the longstanding “duration of status” (D/S) framework for F-1, J-1 and I visa holders.

The court found that the rule “clearly failed to comply with the APA [Administrative Procedure Act] in multiple respects” and preliminarily enjoined DHS from taking any further action to implement the regulation pending further order of the court or resolution of the case on the merits. The court denied the plaintiffs’ request to vacate the final rule at this stage, allowing them to renew the request later in the litigation.

Key takeaways:

Court preserves current D/S framework. The U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts’ ruling preserves the current D/S framework under which eligible F-1 students, J-1 exchange visitors and most I visa holders may remain in the United States for the duration of their approved program or assignment.

Sept. 15 effective date and rule implementation postponed. The court postponed the final rule’s Sept. 15, 2026, effective date establishing fixed admission periods for F-1, J-1 and I nonimmigrants and enjoined DHS from taking further steps to implement the rule while litigation continues.

Final Rule likely violates APA. The court concluded that plaintiffs were likely to succeed on their claims that the rule violates the APA showing that DHS failed to adequately analyze the rule’s costs and benefits, meaningfully consider alternatives, respond to significant public comments and establish a rational connection between the rule and its stated objectives.

Preliminary injunction applies broadly. The injunction applies broadly to the final rule rather than only to the named plaintiffs, with the court finding, “[i]n this case, nationwide relief — which, again, is permitted by § 705 — prevents chaos and confusion that a party-specific order would inevitably generate.”

Additional information: The challenged rule, published on July 17, 2026, would have imposed a four-year admission limit on most F-1 students and J-1 exchange visitors, and a 240-day admission limit on I visa holders, with extensions requiring discretionary DHS approval.

The government is expected to appeal the ruling. BAL will continue to monitor developments as this litigation progresses and will provide updates as additional information becomes available.

This alert has been provided by the BAL U.S. Practice Group.

Maine has joined a multistate lawsuit challenging a rule change by the Trump administration that would make it easier for immigration officials to deny green cards to applicants who have received public benefits.

Federal officials have long had the authority to consider whether an applicant for entry or permanent status would become a "public charge," in the language of the Immigration Act of 1882.

In a lawsuit filed in federal court in New York Monday, the coalition of states said that for over a century, "public charge" has been defined as someone who would or had become primarily dependent on the government for "long term subsistence."

Now, they said a new rule rescinding those guidelines gives immigration officers unfettered authority to deny legal immigration pathways for the use of any public benefit for any period of time.

The states argue the administration overstepped its authority in changing the rule without consulting Congress, and rushed it through without proper notice.

Maine Attorney General Aaron Frey has joined dozens of similar coalition lawsuits since the beginning of the second Trump administration, as Democratic attorneys general have banded together to challenge federal policy changes.

text:
Stanford Health Policy’s Paul Wise, MD, MPH, has been appointed by a federal judge as an independent monitor of immigration detention centers amid allegations that children are being held in unsafe and unsanitary conditions—and for far longer than a court settlement allows.

Dolly M. Gee, chief judge for the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, called on Wise, a professor of pediatrics and health policy, to provide oversight of the children being detained at Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CPB) facilities in Texas and California. Gee also appointed former U.S. Attorney Andrea Sheridan Ordin, as a special master alongside Wise.

The federal judge mandated that the two monitor children in three CBP sections: the Rio Grande Valley, El Paso and San Diego, large areas that account for most of the migrants who have been encountered at the Southwest border.

“My role as the independent monitor is to ensure that Customs and Border Protection and ICE are providing children in custody with a safe and sanitary environment,” said Wise, the Richard E. Behrman Professor of Child Health and Society at Stanford Medicine, a senior fellow at the Freeman Spogli Institute for International Studies and a core faculty member at the Center on Democracy, Development and the Rule of Law.

“This includes food, sleep conditions, medical care, hygiene and sanitation, temperature, and a relatively short time in custody,” Wise said, adding that he is restricted from publicly commenting on his findings, though the judge may eventually release his reports.

The Flores Agreement

In her court order, Gee said the treatment of children in these facilities have not met the requirements of the Flores Settlement Agreement (FSA), a 1997 court-approved settlement that set minimum standards for how immigration authorities treat children in custody. It requires that anyone under 18 be released without unnecessary delay and held in “safe and sanitary” conditions with adequate food, water, and medical care. It also calls on federal immigration officials to treat children with “dignity, respect and special concern for their particular vulnerability as minors.”

Flores is not a law, but a settlement reached to end a lawsuit filed in 1985 on behalf of a 15-year-old Salvadoran girl held in an adult detention facility. Courts have read the agreement to bar the government from holding immigrant children in unlicensed facilities for more than 20 days—a limit the government itself proposed in 2015 and is now arguing does not exist.

The Trump administration has twice tried to end Flores, most recently in a motion Gee denied last August. That appeal was argued before the Ninth Circuit in June and remains undecided. In the meantime, the CBP and ICE are bound by the settlement.

There have been numerous reports in the last 18 months about children being separated from their parents, detained for months on end without adequate food and sanitary conditions. Lawyers for the children say their cells are “iceboxes” and lights are left on all night, disrupting their sleep.

Gee noted in her court order that children were held at ICE’s Dilley Immigration Processing Center for averages of 23 to 47.5 days across five straight months; 66 children for over 80 days in February, and four were held for more than 100 days.

In this video, Wise talks about his work in global hotspots in an effort to protect children in conflict.

Detainment Trauma

“Prior studies have shown that prolonged time in custody can be traumatic for children,” said Wise, an expert on children in conflict who has traveled to many hotspots around the world to advocate on their behalf.

He said the severity of the trauma depends on age, detention without family members, the time in custody and the conditions of detention.

Therefore, he said, “the detention of children should be avoided; however, if policy mandates detention, the time in custody should be short and the conditions appropriate for high-quality care of children."

Gee notes in her order, however, that parents and child advocates, have filed 64 medical grievances at Dilley over 10 months—none resolved in the detainee’s favor.

“Families commonly report ineffective medical care such as children only receiving Tylenol or Ibuprofen in response to various medical needs,” Gee wrote, adding that the parents of a 2-year-old reported that their daughter had a respiratory issues for months, was vomiting and had diarrhea, but all she was given was Tylenol and allergy medication.

A 10-year-old with a heart murmur waited nearly 60 days for a cardiologist; a child who needed an emergency appendectomy was left crying in pain.

Defendants contend that ICE is compliant with the FSA requirements for medical care at Dilley. But Gee countered: "At a minimum, the evidence regarding medical care is conflicting and the reported differences in reality are stark.”

Earlier this year, the American Academy of Pediatrics joined 16 other groups in filing an amicus brief calling for the protections of children outlined in the Flores settlement.

The AAP last year honored Wise with its highest recognition, the 2025 Clifford G. Grulee Award, to acknowledge his exceptional service to the AAP and its mission to promote the health and well-being of children.

“It’s discouraging that this monitor role is necessary,” Wise said.” But if one is necessary, it is a privilege to once again fill this role.”

It’s the third time that Gee has called on Wise for his expertise. In 2019, the judge appointed him as a special expert and, in 2022 as the juvenile care monitor, to conduct an independent investigation into health conditions for migrant children at CBP facilities.

Although his role for the court draws upon his academic work, Wise has stressed that his monitor efforts are separate from his position at Stanford.

name: Litigation
title: Immigration Detention Should Not Be Mandatory
description:
Today, tens of thousands of people are held in civil immigration detention without the right to make a case for their release before an immigration judge.
In other words, these noncitizens remain incarcerated with no access to a fair day in court for a bond hearing, subject to mandatory detention.
History of mandatory detention Detention has not always played such a central role in our immigration system, however.
As mass incarceration exploded in the United States in the criminal legal context, so too did mandatory immigrant detention.
Federal courts push back on expanding mandatory detention As the Trump administration continues to expand the use of mandatory detention, most federal courts across the country have pushed back.
text:
Grandmothers, legal permanent residents, community members with old, nonviolent convictions who have lived in the United States for decades, and even individuals with no criminal record at all — these are the people currently trapped in horrific conditions inside immigrant detention centers across the country.

Today, tens of thousands of people are held in civil immigration detention without the right to make a case for their release before an immigration judge. In other words, these noncitizens remain incarcerated with no access to a fair day in court for a bond hearing, subject to mandatory detention. The only way they can fight for release is to file a habeas petition in federal court, which forces the government to prove it has the legal authority to keep someone locked up. The Trump administration’s relentless enforcement agenda — which spiked the number of people in immigration custody to more than 60,000 as of July 2026 — has resulted in over 70,000 habeas petitions filed in federal courts. And the lack of a bond hearing has resulted in untold numbers of people being unlawfully detained and even wrongfully deported.

Recent expansion of mandatory detention

For the last 30 years, immigration law has made detention the default for two groups of noncitizens: those who recently entered and are seeking admission to the United States, and those with certain criminal convictions. The Trump administration has exponentially increased the use and reach of immigrant detention by weaponizing two statutory provisions: §§ 235(b) and 236(c) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA).

Section 235(b) mandates detention without a bond hearing for noncitizens who have not been admitted to the country and who are “seeking admission” into the United States. The Trump administration recently re-interpreted this provision to cover not only those apprehended while arriving in the U.S., but also anyone who has ever entered the U.S. without inspection — even when they have lived in the U.S. for decades. This means that for the first time, the government is imposing mandatory detention on hundreds of thousands of noncitizens who pose no public safety threat and have deep ties to the country, thereby depriving them of basic due process — merely because they have not been “admitted” under our immigration laws.

Section 236(c), which Congress expanded last year, subjects immigrants with past criminal convictions ranging from minor, nonviolent offenses to crimes like murder, to detention without the opportunity for a bond hearing.

History of mandatory detention

Detention has not always played such a central role in our immigration system, however. The use of detention in the civil immigration system expanded markedly only in recent decades. In the late 1970s, when Haitians were fleeing the Duvalier regime, the U.S. government refused to release Haitian asylum seekers, vastly increasing the number of people in the immigration detention system. By the early 1980s, hundreds of thousands of individuals fleeing Cuba faced a similar fate upon reaching the United States.

Then, Congress in 1988 passed the Anti-Drug Abuse Act, imposing mandatory detention for immigrants convicted of certain aggravated felonies: murder, drug trafficking, and the illegal trafficking of specified firearms and destructive devices.

As mass incarceration exploded in the United States in the criminal legal context, so too did mandatory immigrant detention. The Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 continued expanding the grounds for detention without the possibility of bond, requiring mandatory detention for any noncitizen convicted of most drug offenses and certain firearms offenses. Soon after, the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act widened the definition of aggravated felony and further expanded the basis for mandatory detention to include even minor misdemeanors. This meant that low-level convictions like shoplifting or receipt of a stolen check could subject a noncitizen to immigration detention with no right to a bond hearing — even when those convictions were from decades prior.

Most recently, the Laken Riley Act increased the reach of mandatory detention even further by condemning individuals not only convicted of but charged with or arrested for crimes such as shoplifting to detention without a bond hearing. This latest statutory expansion is the culmination of decades of expanding immigrant detention.

Federal courts push back on expanding mandatory detention

As the Trump administration continues to expand the use of mandatory detention, most federal courts across the country have pushed back. Federal district courts have issued close to 13,000 rulings rejecting the government’s interpretation that § 235(b) applies to immigrants who have been in the U.S. for years, and the majority of courts of appeals echo those rulings. Most recently, the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals joined the growing chorus of circuit courts rejecting the government’s argument that § 235(b) mandates the detention — without opportunity for a bond hearing — of any noncitizen who entered the United States without inspection at any time. A total of nine federal courts of appeal have held the same. Only the Fifth and Eighth circuits have ruled otherwise. This circuit split on § 235(b) is likely to be decided by the Supreme Court.

Meanwhile, the question of whether and when prolonged detention without a bond hearing under § 236(c) violates due process was at the Supreme Court until this month when both parties agreed that the case should be dismissed as moot.

Enforcing immigration laws with due process

Decades of expansion of mandatory detention and the administration’s recent efforts to take this to the extreme has resulted in a system of consequences that treats all immigration violators as dangerous or serious criminals — even when they pose no public safety threat and have deep ties to the United States. The fact that the same punishment is wrought upon a long-time resident with no criminal history and a newly arrived immigrant recently convicted of a violent crime exposes the highly disproportionate nature of the current immigration enforcement system.

Far better frameworks for proportionate responses to violations of the law exist and must be enacted to break the continued expansion of immigrant detention as a one-size-fits-all enforcement tactic. Enforcement responses to violations of the law must be measured, appropriate, and provide any person subject to detention the right to a day in court to make a case for their release.

text:
On September 14, government institutions throughout the Pacific Northwest joined together in a court filing aimed at challenging the federal government’s attempt to apply anti-DEI, anti-immigrant, anti-LGBTQ+, and anti-abortion directives as requirements for receiving funding appropriated by Congress. The new lawsuit, Port of Seattle, et al. v. Blanche, et al., is a follow-on to Martin Luther King, Jr. County, et al., v. Scott Turner, et al., which to date has protected hundreds of millions of dollars in King County alone.

“The Port of Seattle is fighting the Trump Administration’s effort to undermine the award-winning and effective programs that expand opportunity to everyone in our community,” said Port of Seattle Commission President Ryan Calkins. “This region continues to demonstrate the effectiveness of inclusive public service, with federal funding essential to the Port’s operations — including Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, which serves nearly 53 million travelers annually. As a catalyst for more than 204,000 jobs, the Port pursues critical federal resources to support safety, security, and efficient operations. We stand with regional partners in opposing measures that unjustly restrict access to essential funding and will continue to assert our legal rights and defend the interests of our communities against arbitrary federal actions.”

“We have recently fought — and won — similar lawsuits to protect hundreds of millions of dollars for King County,” said King County Prosecuting Attorney Leesa Manion. “The court has been clear: there is no legal basis for the President to impose anti-immigrant, anti-LGBTQ+, and anti-abortion directives as a prerequisite to receive congressionally authorized funding. We will fight to protect these critical resources for public safety, environmental protection, and emergency preparedness in King County, and we are confident we will prevail.”

“The Trump administration continues to try to use federal funding as a weapon to force local governments to compromise on their values and adopt its harmful ideologies,” said King County Executive Girmay Zahilay. “Here in King County, we will not be bullied into choosing between the funding our communities rely on and being a welcoming, inclusive place for all people. We will keep standing up to protect our residents and push back against these unlawful attempts to undermine local authority.”

“Snohomish County has joined multiple lawsuits, including Port of Seattle v. Blanche filed September 14, to protect critical services in our community that have been put at risk due to unlawful conditions placed on federal funding,” said Snohomish County Executive Dave Somers. “The Trump administration seeks to use these vital federal taxpayer dollars as a lever to force compliance with controversial executive orders related to immigration status, health care, and diversity, equity, and inclusion efforts. In this suit, we are challenging untenable conditions on funding that supports an array of public services in our county, including wildfire prevention and response, support for crime victims and witnesses, and work to address environmental and flood mitigation needs along Snohomish County’s shorelines.”

“Federal courts have repeatedly enjoined President Trump’s unlawful attempts to usurp the powers granted to Congress by threatening to withhold federal funding to punish communities that refuse accept his policy agenda,” said Paul Lawrence, who is leading the Pacifica Law Group litigation team representing the plaintiffs. “We are proud to stand alongside this coalition of Washington governments fighting for lawful access to federal resources for their constituents.”

The federal funds at stake in this litigation are resources awarded to local governments by Congress and in which our agencies have met all required conditions, but then the President attempted to revise the terms in order to advance federal directives such as forcing local police agencies to support federal civil immigration. Resources in question include public transportation, public safety, emergency preparedness, environmental protection, flood risk reduction, agricultural assistance, parks and recreation, public health, and housing.

Plaintiffs include the Port of Seattle, Martin Luther King Jr. County, Thurston County, City of Bellingham, Snohomish County, City of Bremerton, and Kitsap County. The case challenges the efforts of the Departments of Justice (DOJ), Homeland Security (DHS), Commerce, Agriculture (USDA), Energy (DOE), Labor (DOL), Interior, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP), and the Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS) to incorporate various grant conditions from Trump Administration executive orders.

Just last month, the Ninth Circuit substantially upheld an injunction against similar conditions in Martin Luther King, Jr. County, et al., v. Scott Turner, et al., in which King County challenged conditions attached to grants by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and U.S. Department of Transport (DOT). Consistent with that authority, the local governments here seek an order declaring the grant conditions at issue unlawful, void, and unenforceable and enjoining their imposition and enforcement.

Now that the complaint has been filed, it is anticipated that the next step will be a court motion for a preliminary injunction in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Washington.

See the version of this release published on Medium by the King County Prosecuting Attorney’s Office.

text:
People packed the Philadelphia Parking Authority’s Market Street boardroom Tuesday morning to voice opposition to a variety of policies, and most of all, the PPA’s parking contract with the Department of Homeland Security.

In September 2025, the PPA entered into a one-year contract with DHS to provide 16 indoor parking spaces for $53,520.

The contract has become the focus of protests calling on the parking authority to cut ties with the federal agency, which oversees Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“I was raised to think, ‘How will our actions be judged by our descendants?’” said Rev. Jay Bergen, a pastor at Germantown Mennonite Church and volunteer with NO ICE Philadelphia.

“I’d rather not be here today,” they stated, “but I am because I am accountable to the congregation I serve, my family and my 2-year-old nephew who, in a few years, will ask, ‘What did you do while ICE agents rounded up your neighbors?’”

The cost of ICE maintaining parking for 16 vehicles in Philadelphia, Bergen argued, far outweighs whatever potential actions the Trump administration may take in response to a nonrenewal of contract.

However, Bergen reiterated a fact that is difficult to overlook: Philadelphia has taken an increasingly strong stance against ICE, recently passing a sweeping package of legislation aimed at limiting the federal agency’s operations and the city’s cooperation with it.

Jack McCurnin, who works with intellectually disabled individuals in Langhorne, Pennsylvania, said ICE’s continued presence in Philadelphia’s suburbs has had a negative effect on its population.

“ICE, through their offices in Philly, harasses multiple of my residents and their families,” McCurnin said.

“I want you to imagine that you cannot speak, that you’re not from this country,” he said. ”Now, you’ve got an agent of the state; you don’t know what they are; nobody’s explained because they don’t think you can understand. You can’t say words, but you can feel it.”

In all, around a dozen anti-ICE activists attended the meeting. Others who spoke included Miriam Oppenheimer, the granddaughter of Holocaust survivors, who likened ICE’s activities in Philadelphia to those of the Gestapo in Nazi Germany.

The PPA’s contract with DHS expires on Sept. 29. Despite the looming date, it remains unclear what the PPA will do come the end of the month.

Criticism over red light cameras

Also contentious was the PPA’s new red light camera program, which, according to data presented during the board meeting, is on track to generate tens of millions of dollars in revenue this year.

Wanda Walker, a Germantown teacher and entrepreneur, expressed doubt over the intentions of the PPA’s ever-expanding speed camera program.

“If it was about safety, they wouldn’t reduce the speed [limit] and then put up the camera. That’s a setup,” she said.

According to data presented during the meeting, areas where cameras have been installed have seen a 67% reduction in speeding incidents, which the PPA characterized as irrefutable proof of success.

Walker has spent considerable time researching PPA policy and networking with individuals negatively affected by what she views as excessive and arbitrary enforcement.

She recounted one story in which a mother and daughter had their cars impounded the same weekend. Because of financial circumstances, the women couldn’t reclaim their vehicles, which were eventually sold.

PPA policy is to initiate the sale of any unclaimed and impounded vehicles after 21 days.

“People’s lives and safety depend on their cars,” Walker said. “It’s as serious as it gets.”

A common theme of community members’ statements was that the PPA is simply out of step with Philadelphia’s population.

Whether regarding parking spaces sold for less than the market price for a historically unpopular law enforcement agency, fines disproportionate to Philadelphians’ income or new speed cameras in low-income areas, all speakers agreed: The PPA must make meaningful changes, and quickly.

title: Immigration Policy Divides Us. Whether to Show Up for People Hurt by it Shouldn't.
description:
Pierre Ronal Bel’s son, Pierre Damas Bel, a 20-year-old neuroscience student, had walked into traffic and died on Aug. 31.
His family believes it was a suicide and says Pierre Damas Bel grew increasingly despondent after ICE fitted him with an ankle monitor.
In Springfield, Ohio, hundreds of volunteers are showing that it is.
You and I can disagree on immigration policy while agreeing that Pierre Damas Bel’s death is a tragedy and feeling compassion for Pierre’s family’s suffering.
We can disagree on temporary protected status decisions yet still understand the fears that immigrant communities across the country are navigating.
text:
(RNS) — At 3 a.m., my daughter shook me awake. She had a nightmare and needed snuggles and reassurances she was safe. I held her until the dark no longer seemed so scary.

Hundreds of miles away, in Springfield, Ohio, Pastor Carl Ruby was holding someone too — not a frightened child, but a grieving father. Pierre Ronal Bel’s son, Pierre Damas Bel, a 20-year-old neuroscience student, had walked into traffic and died on Aug. 31. His family believes it was a suicide and says Pierre Damas Bel grew increasingly despondent after ICE fitted him with an ankle monitor. “Everything was fine with him before this happened,” his father told “The New York Times.”

This is not the only tragedy impacting the Haitian immigrant communities in Ohio. Since the U.S. government removed temporary protected status for Haitians a few weeks ago, ICE has stepped up enforcement. Local advocates have raised concerns about potential family separations for over 1,200 U.S.-born children in Springfield who have Haitian parents.

My organization’s work is bringing people together across religious divides — and in the face of a humanitarian crisis like this, it’s fair to ask whether cooperation across difference actually is even possible.

In Springfield, Ohio, hundreds of volunteers are showing that it is. Recently, hundreds of volunteers from a range of faith communities —Baptists, Unitarian Universalists, Mennonites, Quakers and others — packed meals for Haitian residents too afraid to leave their homes. They also lobbied political leaders to call for the release of two Haitian pastors who had been detained by ICE, and they stood outside Haitian houses of worship to protect their right to worship without fear.

For anyone who looks, there are signs that pluralism — the simple and quintessentially American idea that we can cooperate across difference for the common good — is alive in communities across the nation. Neighbors show up for one another, providing comfort and food and working to protect basic human rights and dignities.

Pluralism allows for respectful disagreement without letting that disagreement define the relationships. You and I can disagree on immigration policy while agreeing that Pierre Damas Bel’s death is a tragedy and feeling compassion for Pierre’s family’s suffering. We can disagree on temporary protected status decisions yet still understand the fears that immigrant communities across the country are navigating. If we put an increased focus on what we agree upon — re-anchor ourselves in shared humanity, rather than disagreement — we might, over time, find it easier to resolve our disagreements.

I understand if disagreements over the current immigration crisis seems like “long bridges,” insurmountable differences to cross. But even on these hard issues, I believe pluralism can be a solution. Pluralism is the simple invitation to widen the welcome and focus on common ground with an expanding range of potential partners. I see pluralism at work in community responses to the immigration crisis with churches, mosques and synagogues forging new relationships to live out their deeply held religious values, despite the other issues that may deeply divide them.

My own congregation in Maryland, in partnership with other religious and community groups, is hosting a set of legal clinics for local immigrant communities. The focus is not on particular policy outcomes but on the idea that the inherent worth and dignity of every person means everyone deserves excellent legal advice contextualized for their particular needs. These clinics have brought together Maryland residents who have never previously met but share that value and feel called to live it out with their neighbors.

As a parent, my heart aches for Pierre’s family and the pain so many other immigrant families are experiencing. We have seen the moral disasters that dehumanization leads to throughout history. The tradition of pluralism gives us a pathway to humanize one another, living up to the shared value of human dignity emphasized across diverse religious traditions. It is also an invitation to live into our national aspiration of “e pluribus unum”: out of many, one.
